en: *Jingming jing jijie guanzhong shu*, Scroll One,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Daoyi of Zisheng Monastery in the Capital. In the past, during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han,
the Dharma teachings first began to flow into the region of Congzuo (Gansu), where pagodas and images were first established and scriptures were translated.
Furthermore, there were obstacles;
even when reaching the Wei and Jin dynasties, although translations were initiated and propagated, the various scriptures produced were still characterized by sparse diction and convoluted reasoning.
This was likely because those who studied them had not yet attained a comprehensive perspective on the Great View.
The translators lacked proficiency in local dialects;
since they served as intermediaries for the subtle and profound Great Dharma, it is impossible to measure their successes and failures.
It was from the winter of the third year of Hongshi of the Qin dynasty that Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong.
Previously, he translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, as well as the *Śata-śāstra* and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, thereby immersing himself in the ultimate truth.
Only after this did he retranslate this sutra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and others;
thus, the phrasing is incisive and the principles reach their consummation, leaving nothing to be desired.

It is said that the transmission and practice have long been sparse; the Way has prioritized study, leading to the heterodox being treated as distinct, which has caused the Great Tradition to become overgrown and the True Ultimate to wither.
Now, the preliminary formulations from Guanzhong are concise in expression yet profound in meaning, and are intended for transmission.
Later students may find it difficult to penetrate due to its brevity;
this is likely because times have changed and their understanding has grown dim,
rather than being a deficiency on the part of the former sages.
The Dao-ye, not deeming his own abilities shallow or inadequate,
has ventured to supplement and expand upon the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* using Zhi’s commentary as its basis,
and for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he has relied upon Daosheng’s sub-commentary.
Thereafter, I sought out various interpretations from all sides to grasp the common, sublime purport.
Although I have recorded these, I have not produced anything original;
in the end, I am as ashamed as one who lost his sheep.

At that time, in the first year of the Shangyuan era, during the year of Kuntun, and at the beginning of the Yongtai reign, it was once again revised and finalized during the summer retreat at the Bodhi Monastery in Chang’an;
thus may the Dharma-mirror be further clarified and the lamp of wisdom increasingly brightened.
Preface to the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, composed by Shi Sengzhao.
As for the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, it is truly a designation for that which exhausts the subtle and completes transformation, reaching a state of wondrous transcendence.
Its purport is profound and mysterious, beyond the reach of words or forms;
its Way transcends the three emptinesses, beyond the deliberations of those of the two vehicles.
It surpasses the realm of numerical categories and cuts off the sphere of the mind that possesses intentionality.
Vast and profound, it is non-active yet there is nothing it does not do;
it has no knowledge of how things are, yet it is able to make them so—this is the inconceivable. Why is this?
It is because the sagely wisdom is without knowing, yet it illuminates all myriad phenomena simultaneously.
The Dharma-body is formless yet manifests in diverse forms;

it universally responds to the ultimate rhythms and is beyond words, yet its profound teachings are spread far and wide. Its mysterious power acts without deliberation, yet its movements accord with the needs of circumstances. Thus it is said.

It is able to govern and rescue all quarters, opening up things and accomplishing affairs, bringing benefit to manifest throughout the world; yet it remains non-active (*wuwei*). To those who are deluded, its responsive illumination appears as "wisdom" (*zhi*);
when it manifests forms, it is called the "body" (*shen*); and when it is perceived, it is called "vision" (*dian*).
The profound scriptures simply call this "words," and seeing change and movement, they call it "expediency" (quán).
Now, how could the ultimate state of the Way be realized through the forms of words or the wisdom of expediency within its divine realm?
Yet, the multitude have long been in deep slumber, and none but words can awaken them.
The Way does not operate in isolation; its propagation depends upon people.
For this reason, the Tathāgata dispatched Mañjuśrī from a distant land and summoned Vimalakīrti from the earth, so that they might assemble at Vaiśālī and together propagate this Way.
In this sutra, what is elucidated is that, when encompassing all practices, expedient wisdom is primary;
when establishing the roots of virtue, the six perfections are the foundation;
and when rescuing the ignorant and deluded, compassion is foremost.
When speaking of the ultimate essence of the teaching, it is described as non-duality.
All these various doctrines are the foundation of the inconceivable.

As for such matters as borrowing a seat from the King of Lamps, requesting a meal from the Land of Fragrance, taking the great trichiliocosm in one’s hand, or enclosing the heavens and the phenomenal world within a single room—these are the traces of the inconceivable.
However, the profound gate is difficult to open, and the Sage’s responses are not uniform.
Without the fundamental (ben), there would be no way to manifest the traces (ji);
without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental.
Although the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are one and inconceivable;
therefore, he commanded his attendant to record this as its title.
The Celestial King of the Great Qin possesses a spirit that transcends the world and a profound mind uniquely enlightened.
He extended great governance over the myriad affairs of state and propagated the transformation of the Way for a thousand years to come.
Whenever he sought out and perused these scriptures, he regarded them as the dwelling place for the settling of his spirit;
yet, he lamented that the translations produced by Zhi Qian and Dharmarakṣa were hindered by their adherence to the literal text.
I have always feared that the sublime essence of the *xuanzong* might fall into decline due to the translators; yet the destiny of the Northern Heaven has its own time for fulfillment.
In the eighth year of Hongshi, when the year was in the position of Chunchu (the Bird-Fire), I commanded the Great General, Duke of Changshan.

The Right General, Marquis of Ancheng, together with one thousand two hundred śramaṇas of the Institute for the Study of Meaning, invited Dharma Master Kumārajīva at the Great Monastery in Chang’an to retranslate the authentic version.

Kumārajīva, possessing a magnanimity that transcended the world, had settled his mind in the realm of ultimate reality; having fully mastered the "Center of the Circle," he was moreover proficient in local dialects.
At that time, he would hold the foreign text in his hand while personally proclaiming the translation with his own voice.
Both monastics and laypeople were reverent, repeating his words three times over as they refined their understanding through diligent inquiry, striving to preserve the Sage’s intent.
His writing was concise yet profound, and its meaning subtle yet manifest;
thus, the subtle and far-reaching teachings were made clear therein.

Nevertheless, as I have had the misfortune of listening to this in my ignorance for some time, and though I have subsequently contemplated it to penetrate its profound mysteries, I have only roughly grasped the meaning of the text.
I have therefore hastily provided an annotated commentary based on what I heard, briefly recording these sincere words; I have sought to transmit them rather than compose anything of my own.
In the future, gentlemen of later generations shall hear this together.
Regarding the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, Rui said:
"Now, some sutras are named after persons."
Alternatively, as for those named after dharmas,
these are not generally spoken by the Buddha himself;
rather, they are mostly given according to people.
That which the Buddha has taught is not limited to a single sūtra;
therefore, it is named according to the specific teaching expounded therein.
This sūtra combines both the names of the person and the dharma.
To name it after the person clarifies the origin of the Dharma;
to name it after the Dharma summarizes the general structure of the sutra.
This is why both are preserved. Śrīmitra said:
Vimalakīrti— whose name means "Pure Name" in the language of Qin—
is one of five hundred youths who has come from the Land of Wondrous Joy to travel through this realm.
Having completed all that was to be done and being about to return to his native land,
he wished to manifest his pure virtue in order to benefit all living beings; yet,
the manifestation and narration of the essential points of his awakening must necessarily have its underlying cause.
Therefore, while he has sent his fellow practitioners to the Buddha, he alone does not go.
From his failure to go alone, one knows that he is ill.
How is this known?
Five hundred fellow practitioners together follow the Great Way;
in advancing virtue and cultivating goodness, they are invariably united in both motion and stillness.
This assembly for the Pure Land is a great undertaking.
Yet they do not differ in their shared illumination of the existence of illness;
because there is illness, there is a gathering for inquiring after it.
The gathering for inquiring after illness arises from the assembly in the Pure Land.
The assembly in the Pure Land arises through the skillful means of Vimalakīrti;
thus, the very foundation for the beginning and end of this sutra truly lies herein.
If one observes it from the perspective of his own discourse, he is equal to the Sage.
Tracing the merit back to its source, the merit originates with Vimalakīrti.
Since one must investigate its provenance, it is called "The Teaching of Vimalakīrti. Zhaò says:
"Vimalakīrti is, in the language of Qin, 'Pure Name' (Jìngmíng); he is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body."
His expedient path is without fixed form, and his manifestations differ whether he remains hidden or appears.
He departed from that Land of Wondrous Joy to manifest here in this Saha World;
thus, by blending his light with the mundane world, he caused the Way and its teachings to be propagated.
He has always traveled together with Ratnakūṭa as his companion in the city of Dharma.
Now that his teaching mission is completed and he is about to return to Abhirati,
he wishes to manifest his spiritual virtues in order to propagate the Tathāgata’s path of inconceivable liberation.
Finally, Ratnakūṭa alone approached Śākyamuni; thereupon,
[the Buddha] feigned illness to initiate the occasion for inquiring after his health,
thereby establishing the beginning of subtle discourse.
Because these wondrous songs originate from him, his teachings are so named. Sengsheng said:
"Vimalakīrti is, in the Sanskrit language, Vimalakīrti, meaning 'Stainless Renown.
He concealed his traces amidst the five desires yet remained transcendent and untainted; his pure fame spread far and wide."
Therefore, this title was bestowed.
Those who value names and seek their corresponding reality must regard such teachings with gravity;
since these teachings fundamentally express reality, by valuing them one will ultimately attain what is sought.
Because of this, there are statements that approach the errors of the sacred word. The Sūtra:
in Sanskrit it is called *sūtra*, which is translated here as "契" (*qiè*).
This refers to words that accord with principle and teachings that correspond to the faculties [of sentient beings].
Returning from delusion to realize the truth;
the myriad sages follow the same rule.
It is also said:
Because it is eternal.
Master Zhao says that it is the constancy of the principle.
Although the past and present differ, the Way of Awakening does not change.
The multitudes of the heterodox cannot obstruct it;
the assembly of the sages cannot alter it.
It is also named "Inconceivable Liberation. This is a name received according to its dharma-nature.
The following text states:
"The Buddha taught that for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the abandonment of lust, anger, and delusion constitutes liberation.
However, for those without such overweening pride, the very nature of lust and anger [is itself liberation]."
This refers precisely to liberation; this discourse concerns its essence.
Alternatively, from the perspective of compassion and vows, it is called "defiled" or "undefiled," and "non-path" or "path-attaining.
These are names applied according to its function.
In the past, through the provisional teachings, the three vehicles were led by means of the statement that their liberation was identical;
now, as he returns from the provisional to the real,
he specifically designates it as "inconceivable."

Thus, the liberation described in the hundred verses of the *Mahāvaipulya* and the liberations of all the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the *Avataṃsaka* are identical to this. Kumārajīva said:
"It is also called *samādhi*, and it is also called the supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*)."
They may cause things to change their proportions— whether long or short—
or allow the large and small to interpenetrate, transforming according to their will.
Because they exercise mastery over all phenomena and are liberated from all hindrances, they are called "liberated" (vimokṣa).
The Capable One can thus manifest things such that beings do not know why; therefore, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
It is also said:
"When the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body contemplate, they respond according to circumstances without entering meditative absorption."
Only then can one be capable.
Because the mind attains mastery and is no longer bound by incapacity, it is called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
If one were to directly clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), it would contradict habitual practice and provide no basis for gaining conviction.
The manifestation of objects changes according to the mind, clarifying that things have no fixed nature.
Since things have no fixed nature, their nature is empty.
Because the Bodhisattva attains this lack of fixity, he causes objects to revolve according to the mind; this is inconceivable.
This serves as a clear proof of emptiness and reveals the fundamental principle of the school; therefore, it is taken as the heading of the scripture. Zhaò says:
"Subtle, distant, profound, and deep—it is 'inconceivable' (acintya) because the two vehicles cannot fathom it."
Acting with unrestrained freedom, one cannot be constrained by the burdens of worldly dust; this is liberation.
This sutra begins with the Pure Land and concludes with the nourishment of the Dharma.
Although what is elucidated therein differs, the inconceivable liberation is one and the same;
therefore, it is designated by that name as a whole.
Thus, the title of the sutra is derived from the name of a person.
This refers to sutras titled after the Dharma;
they are so designated to indicate their essential purpose.
Those titled after persons are so named because the Way was propagated through them. Sheng said:
Because the appellation "Stainless" might merely refer to outward appearances while leaving the mind uneasy, he further speaks of his liberation;
this serves as yet another name: the "Inconceivable One."
There are generally two kinds.
The first is that the emptiness of principle cannot be grasped by deluded sentiments.
Second: The miraculous and supernatural are not to be measured by those of shallow understanding;
if one realizes the principle of emptiness, one will be liberated from the delusions of conceptual thought.
Once delusion has been shed, one's actions become unfathomable.
Vimalakīrti now displays wonders in both his movement and stillness; he must have certainly shed all delusions.
To shed delusion lies in realizing the emptiness of the self.
It is taught that emptiness is its essential nature.
Therefore, the name "Stainless" is not merely a matter of faith but possesses verifiable evidence.
If there is indeed such evidence, the more one seeks it, the closer one approaches it.
When one arrives before a seeker, what worry is there that they will not attain awakening? Rui said:
"The Bodhisattva has no fixed mind yet responds to things with speech;
sentient beings merely behold the teaching and cannot fathom its underlying cause."
Therefore, that which is spoken of is called "inconceivable.
Although it is spoken, because there is no mind [behind it], it is not obstructed by existence;
although there is no mind, because it is able to speak, it is not obstructed by non-existence.
Because there is nothing that can burden it, it is called liberation.
Chapter One: On the Buddha-land. Kumārajīva said:
The beginning and end of this sutra depend upon the Pure Land.
Therefore, the "Buddha-land" chapter is placed at the beginning of all the sections; therein,
the two lands of the Real and the Responsive are unified through equality,
as will be explained in detail below.
Nevertheless, these fourteen chapters of the sutra are largely divided into three sections.
The first half of this chapter is called the *nidāna* (introductory section), as it is intended to inspire faith in those who have not yet attained it.
The subsequent eleven and a half chapters constitute the *samyag-deśanā* (main body of the teaching), as they are intended to bring about realization for those who have already gained faith.
The latter two sections, which follow after the realization of the entire sūtra, are called the "Section on Dissemination" (pariṇāmanā).
Within the initial "Section on the Introduction" (nidāna), there are again three distinct parts.
The first enumerates the time, place, and other such details.
The compilers of this sutra cite events to provide evidence for its credibility;
subsequently, they manifest the land by closing the canopy.
This is how the expounders of the sutra startle beings into faith.
The subsequent eulogy and praise serve to cause those who inquire about this sutra to look up to its virtue and give rise to faith.
The initial section further consists of six parts.
First, the words of the sutra;
second, the purport of the sutra;
third, the time of hearing the sutra.
Fourth, those who preach the sūtras;
fifth, the places where the sūtras are heard;
sixth, the assemblies that hear the sūtras.
"Thus" (*evam*) refers to the phrasing of this initial scripture of faith.
Zhaò says:
"Thus" refers to the phrasing of faithful compliance.
Now, when there is faith, the principles of what is spoken accord with reality;
when they accord with reality, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected. Whether the scriptures are extensive or concise, they are not transmitted without faith;
therefore, it is said: "One speaks [only] because of this."
"Thus have I heard. These two [phrases] convey the essential meaning of the scripture.
Sengzhao said:
"The one who brought forth the scripture clarifies that he personally received the Sage’s instructions, so as to eliminate any errors of hearsay."
"At one time" refers to the time when these three heard this sutra.
It is called "one time" because sentient beings' faith and reverence constitute the stimulus, while the Tathāgata’s compassionate vow constitutes the response; thus, stimulus and response intersect.
Zhaò says:
This is a time when the auspicious convergence of the Dharma King’s inauguration has occurred.
Regarding these four explanations of the sutra,
in the Sanskrit language they are called:
"Buddha" is fully explained as "the Knower.
As it says in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
Because one knows the true meaning of all phenomena.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Bodhi is named wisdom (*jñāna*)."
The Buddha is called the "Wise One.
This refers to one who possesses perfected virtue through understanding and whose speech is sincere, such that all beings place their trust in him.
He was in Vaiśālī; the following five locations list the places where the sutra was heard.
There is both the general and the specific.
The general serves for those who know from afar; the specific serves for those nearby so that there is no error.
This is the first general location.
Zhaò says:
Vaiśālī is the name of a country;
in the language of Qin, it means "Vast and Majestic."
Its land is level, vast, and adorned; it is named after these qualities.
It is also said that the soil is well-suited for fine rice.
The *āmra* tree is round; it is located in a separate place.
Zhaò says:
"Āmra" is the name of the tree.
That fruit resembles a peach but is not one;
the previous mention of the "Nai" (Anana) family was an error.
This matter is found in another sutra.
"Monastery" (*ārāma*) is a general term for a place of residence.
In Sanskrit it is called *saṃghārāma*,
which here means "garden of the community."
The term "ārāma" (伽藍) is an abbreviation.

"Together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus"—the following six items list the assembly that heard the sutra together, serving as evidence that this is not a mistaken transmission; there are three distinct categories among this assembly.
First, the śrāvakas are listed.
Because they excel both in form and mind and possess the most intimate realization and faith, they are listed first.
Next, the bodhisattvas are listed.
Their minds are the same but their forms differ; because their testimony and faith are somewhat sparse, they are listed next.
Finally, the devas and nāgas are listed;
because both their forms and minds are discordant, their testimony and faith are most sparse, and thus they are listed last.
The initial listing of "bhikṣus" indicates those who share [the precepts].
"Great" refers to the ultimate fruit; "bhikṣu" is the name for a person, and "assembly" refers to their collective harmony.
Zhaò says:
"Bhikṣu" is translated in the Qin language as "Pure Alms-seeker," or "Destroyer of Afflictions," or "One Capable of Upholding the Precepts."
He is also named "Able to Terrify Māra.
In India, a single name encompasses these four meanings;
since there was no single corresponding term in the Qin language to translate it, its meaning-based name has been retained.
"Bodhisattvas": the following two columns list the assembly of bodhisattvas.
This section has five parts;
first, the enumeration of their names.
Second, the enumeration;
third, the praise of virtues;
fourth, the listing of names.
Fifth, the general conclusion.
This is the first [section]. Zhaò says:
The correct phonetic transcription of "Bodhisattva" is *bodhisattva*.
*Bodhi* means the Buddha-way;
*sattva*, in the language of Qin (Chinese), means "great mind."
Sentient beings possess a great mind that enters the Buddha-way.
This is so called because they seek the Way for the sake of all beings through great compassion, wisdom, and boundless practices and vows.
Kumārajīva said:
There are generally three kinds of Mahāsattvas:
first, those who have left the household life;
second, those who remain in the household life.
Third, those who come from other directions.
Furthermore, first is the body of karmic retribution;
second is the dharma-body.
Among these, the bodhisattva is for the most part the Dharma-body;
nevertheless, the form manifested in response shares the same traces as material objects,
such that sentient beings may perceive it as being on equal footing with them.
Because they might conceive an inferior notion [of the number], he cites a large figure;
thereafter, he enumerates the virtues.
"Thirty-two thousand" refers to the second category of enumeration.
"Known by all"—the following three sections praise his virtues.
The text has three parts;
first is the general praise.
Next is the specific praise;
then follows the concluding praise.
Furthermore, the general praise consists of three parts.
This first section praises his external transformation.
Hearing his name and admiring his reputation constitutes "knowing" him;
beholding his form and drinking in his transformative influence constitutes "perceiving" him.
Sengzhao said:
"The Great Being abides in the world like the sun and moon rising in the sky;
what person with eyes would not recognize him?"
"Having fully accomplished all the fundamental practices of great wisdom"—this is the second, the practice of self-cultivation.
"Great wisdom praises the understanding, and the fundamental practices praise the conduct.
Zhaò says:
Great wisdom is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This wisdom takes the practices of the six perfections and the six supernormal powers as its foundation.
All great beings have already perfected these fundamental practices.
"Established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas"—this is the third explanation of the title.
Zhaò says:
"The grace of Heaven is impartial."
It does not moisten withered wood.
Although the Buddha’s majesty is universal, it does not take root where there is no foundation.
For that which is established, the roots of the Way must necessarily be deep.
Ei said: "In general, there are two kinds.
Either, by applying spiritual transformation, one causes them to attain momentary awakening; this is termed 'establishment' (kengyō)."
Alternatively, to open their minds with the sublime Dharma and transform them so that they become like oneself is also called "establishment.
To protect the city of the Dharma and uphold the true Dharma—hereafter follows the second section, which explains the specific praise in three parts.
First, it is praised by way of protecting the Dharma;
next, it is praised by way of practice;
finally, it is praised by way of the proximate fruit.
The initial text also has three parts:
namely, the protection of the Dharma and the protection of persons.
Explanation of the connection:
The protection of the Dharma further consists of two parts;
this first section praises the cultivation of its causes.
Zhaò said:
"Externally, it serves as a city wall for protecting the Dharma;
internally, it possesses the firmness of upholding and maintaining it."
Kumārajīva said:
"The 'Dharma-city' refers to the Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
It is called 'protection' because it causes sentient beings to have no divergent views."
Furthermore, all the teachings of the sūtras are called the "Dharma City.
One must protect and proclaim them so that they do not fall into ruin;
those who are able to uphold the True Dharma should also concurrently guard it.
Ei said: "Ultimate truth is the Dharma; written words are the city.
When the moats and ramparts of the city are firm, those within are not harmed."
When the words remain, the principle is not lost.
To be able to roar the lion’s roar so that one's fame is heard throughout the ten directions—this second [part] praises the accomplishment of merit.
Zhaò said:
The "lion's roar" is the sound of fearlessness.
Whatever one proclaims, being unafraid of the various heterodoxies and rival schools,
is likened to the lion's roar.
Because he descends among the various beasts and his practice fills the world, it is said that there is nowhere he does not reach universally.
That he brings peace to people without being asked as their friend—these two are praises of his protection of beings. Furthermore, there are two [aspects to each].
This first praises the mind.
Zhaò says:
"A true friend does not wait to be invited."
It is like a compassionate mother hastening to her infant.
To perpetuate and exalt the Three Jewels so that they do not cease—this is the second praise for the perfection of his merit.
Zhaò says: "To continue the lineage of the Buddha is to cause the Three Jewels to flourish."
It is not merely a matter of clearly manifesting the Three Jewels and proclaiming the circulation of the sutras and the Dharma;
it means that one can accumulate goodness and build up merit until one spontaneously attains Buddhahood.
If one attains Buddhahood, then there is the Dharma;
if there is the Dharma, then there is the Sangha.
The merit of ensuring these do not cease shall persist through future kalpas.
Now, if one speaks of non-interruption, it must mean that one is capable;
furthermore, within this interval, one practices it oneself and transforms others,
while those others likewise transform sentient beings.
When both things and the self are perfected, the Three Jewels flourish extensively;
because sentient beings are inexhaustible, the Jewels likewise never cease.
"Subduing the maras and enemies and restraining all heterodox paths"—these three explanations constitute the eulogy.
Zhaò says:
"Māra" refers to the four Māras;
"non-Buddhists" refers to the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths.
Tiantai said:
"Through meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), one subdues craving and attains supernatural powers;
through wisdom (prajñā), one destroys [wrong] views and thereby subdues the various māras."
He develops eloquence to refute the heterodox schools, as clarified in the "Inquiry into Ailments" chapter.
All of this is for the sake of purity; the following two sections are praises of spiritual practice.
This consists of two distinct parts: one's own practice and the transformation of others.
Within the former—self-practice—there are again two sections;
the first praises the virtue of abandonment.
Next, there is the praise of his qualities of wisdom.
Regarding the text on the qualities of abandonment, there are three sections;
this first part is a general praise.
"Forever free from the hindrances and entanglements"—this is the second specific praise.
Zhaò says: "The 'hindrances' refer to the five hindrances."
There are ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
and there are also immeasurable envelopments.
When the body, speech, and mind are pure— such that the three karmas are entirely purified— the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and envelopments cannot burden one.
The five hindrances are:
first, the hindrance of sensual desire;
second, the hindrance of ill will.
3. The hindrance of sloth and torpor;
4. The hindrance of restlessness and remorse;
5. The hindrance of doubt.
The first two [hindrances] obstruct morality;
sleepiness obstructs wisdom;
and restlessness and regret obstruct concentration.
Doubt obstructs liberation as well as knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

The ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*). Yì said:
In ordinary beings, the fetters are merely suppressed; they cease for a time but arise again.
In those of the Two Vehicles, though difficult to extinguish, the locus of realization still persists.

In the Great Being, who realizes emptiness, both mind and sensory objects are simultaneously stilled; where cessation occurs, the roots of existence are utterly extinguished, leaving nothing upon which birth can depend.
It is said thus because the Dharma-body is fundamentally beyond discussion.
"The mind constantly dwells in unimpeded liberation" is the third concluding praise.
Kumārajīva said:
The "inconceivable liberation" (acintya-vimokṣa) is precisely of this category;
it is so named because there is no obstruction regarding phenomena. Sengzhao says:
"That which is attained at the seventh stage is this liberation; because one then penetrates all dharmas without hindrance, the mind dwells in constant tranquility."
"Mindfulness, concentration, and eloquence are uninterrupted throughout all times. This section below praises his wisdom-virtue, which also consists of three parts;
this is the first, a general praise.
Zhaò says:
Mindfulness is right mindfulness;
concentration is right concentration.
Through dhāraṇī, one maintains the good without loss and prevents the arising of evil.
There is no leakage.
"Recollection" refers to *dhāraṇī* (total retention) and the sevenfold eloquence (*saptapratibhāna*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
First, swift eloquence;
second, beneficial eloquence;
third, inexhaustible eloquence.
Fourth, the eloquence of non-interruption;
fifth, the eloquence of appropriate discernment;
sixth, the eloquence of meaning.
These seven are the supreme eloquences in the world;
these four are the essential requirements of a Great Being, and therefore they are never interrupted.
Ei said: "If mindfulness is not forgotten, wisdom will increase ever further;
if concentration is not abandoned, the mind will remain constantly unified."
If one maintains the good without losing it, then memory and awareness will be strong and evil will not arise.
If eloquence is uninterrupted, then transformation will be unimpeded and complete.
These four gates can govern all myriad practices; therefore, they are so called.
Kumārajīva said:
"When a bodhisattva attains these four dharmas,
they enter deeply into the firm and solid body of the sūtra without losing it."
Because his realization has become increasingly luminous throughout successive kalpas, it is said that it is uninterrupted.

He is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means. Second, this is a specific praise of his merit of wisdom.
Sengzhao said:

"Perfection refers to the practice of signlessness (*animitta*). From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the mental faculty is quiescent; because the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no virtue that is not enacted.
Therefore, although giving reaches its ultimate limit in giving, one never actually gives."
Precepts reach their ultimate limit in precepts, yet one has never practiced them as precepts.

It is called wisdom because it is without cognition yet there is nothing it does not know regarding the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
Although they have realized the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are able to refrain from realizing [nirvāṇa].
Abiding in existence, they do not lose non-existence;
dwelling in non-existence, they do not abandon existence.

Reaching the stage of non-attainment and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—this is the third section, which concludes by way of the stages.

"Having already been able to accord with and turn the non-retrogressive wheel"—the following two lines clarify the practice of transforming others. This section has two parts:

The continuous unfolding of perfect penetration, which is not restricted to a single person, is called the Wheel [of Dharma].

Being skilled in understanding the characteristics of dharmas and knowing the faculties and natures of sentient beings—this second explanation concerns their capacity to turn [the wheel] accordingly.
Sengzhao said:

This means that by knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, one is able to act accordingly.

The physical form is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;

Adorning the form is the means by which one transcends the mundane world.
Furthermore, it is merely to manifest a majestic appearance for those who perceive him as a venerable form;

His fame and reputation are loftily remote, surpassing Mount Sumeru. This section below clarifies the third excellence: possessing a renowned name.

This section has two parts.

how much more so should the preaching of the Dharma accord with the faculties [of beings] to universally produce wholesome states in all living beings.
Zhaò says:
The light of the Dharma-treasure shines upon all without exception;

Its moisture wets all without exception.
It moistens birth and death.
It is likened to a divine treasure in the ocean that can emit light to dispel darkness.
Furthermore, it is because of this light that nectar can rain down to moisten what is withered.
Regarding the phrase "the most subtle and supreme among all vocal sounds": this refers to the union of two factors.

Sengzhao said:

he has deeply penetrated dependent origination and severed all false views."
The third explanation is that there are no further habitual tendencies regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

None of these are profound.
The Bodhisattva awakens to the fact that birth is not birth,

He expounds the Dharma without fear, like the roar of a lion.

Thus, Vasubandhu said:

just as the spring thunder stirs the hundred grasses."

"Gathering the dharma-treasures of the assembly like a sea-leader"—the following section clarifies the benefits of attaining the fruit in three parts. The text is divided into two [sections].
This first section establishes the metaphor of the Guide obtaining the treasure.
The six heterodox teachers provide false guidance and fail to attain the true fruit;
because the Eightfold Path benefits beings and leads inevitably to Nirvana, this metaphor is employed.
Zhaò said:
"To guide sentient beings into the ocean of the Mahāyāna,
gathering the various jewels of the Dharma so that they may surely obtain them without difficulty."
Just as a skilled maritime captain leads merchants so that they surely obtain the *maṇi* gem,

one who thoroughly understands the profound and subtle meaning of all phenomena and well knows the destinations of beings' coming and going as well as the movements of their minds— this latter pair of explanations [indicates] the reason for being able to lead, because of being endowed with both skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
With wisdom that penetrates profound meanings, one is able to abide in bodhi;
through skillful means, one realizes that the coming and going of sentient beings is like an illusion.
Thus, while compassion benefits sentient beings, things cannot impair the virtue of the Mahāsattva.
This is precisely what is meant here.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Wisdom does not apprehend existence or non-existence, yet it gives rise to the mind of great compassion."

"Approaching the peerless wisdom of the Buddha’s sovereignty, fearless in the ten directions, and possessing the eighteen unique qualities"—this first section clarifies self-realization, praising his virtues as the proximate fruit of the three supernormal knowledges (*vidyā*).
The text has three parts; this is the first.
Sengzhao said:
"The Buddha-way is transcendent and peerless;
because only the Buddha is equal to himself, it is called 'unequaled' (asama-sama)."
The reason for distinguishing their equality is to clarify that the single Great Principle reaches its ultimate limit in everything;
it is as level as empty space—
how could there be any rising or falling within it?
The sovereign wisdom consists precisely of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities.
Although the Great Being has not yet fully realized the Buddha’s wisdom, he is already close to it; he has closed the gates to all evil realms of existence.
"And yet he is born into the five destinies to manifest his body. This section clarifies the benefits of transformation and has two parts:
first, it clarifies being born without being born;
second, it clarifies responding to birth to benefit sentient beings.

Because this is the initial realization of the signless (*animitta*), the various realms of existence are naturally closed off; yet, without abandoning great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one manifests birth within the five destinies. The "five destinies" consist of the three [evil] paths, as well as humans and devas.
Zhaò says:
The Dharma-body is without birth, yet there is nothing that is not born.

because there is nothing that is not born, it manifests birth within the five destinies.
He acts as a great king of physicians, skillfully healing all ailments;

The text has four parts.

There is no virtue that is not complete;
all immeasurable Buddha-lands are adorned and purified. This refers to the fulfillment of the secondary environment (*pratyaya-sampad*).
Zhaò says:
Sentient beings are infinite and their preferences differ;
therefore, one cultivates immeasurable pure lands to respond to those diverse inclinations.
Those who see or hear [of them] will all receive benefit. Third, the virtue of benefiting sentient beings is perfected.

How could there be seeing and hearing that provides no benefit?"
Ei said: "The Dharma-body has no body;
because it has no body, it responds only after being stimulated."
If one responds only after being moved, there will be no response that does not accord with the occasion;
thus, it ensures that all who see or hear [the teaching] receive benefit, and whatever is performed is never in vain.
Fourth, the virtue of one's own practice is perfected.
Sengzhao said:
"Merit is not established in vain.

The Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Being unconditioned, it does not act according to its own will; because it does not act according to its own will, its movements never occur at an improper time.
Since its movements never occur at an improper time, all that it undertakes is likewise never in vain.
"In this way, they are all fully endowed with every merit"—this is the third summary.

he appears as one who bends down without harming any creature.

"Muditendriya means 'joyful faculty' (mudita = joy)."

Regarding the Bodhisattva Raticandra, Kumārajīva says:
"Joy is of two kinds."

second is the joy of the pure Dharma, for which reason he is called the "King.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Bianyin, Kumārajīva said:
"Words are eloquence.

Bodhisattva Holding the Precious Torch:

Bodhisattva Jewel Courage: Kumārajīva says...

Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnapratibhāsa, Kumārajīva said:

Wuyuan Guan Bodhisattva: Kumārajīva says—

"Jī" (積) means "to accumulate wisdom."
Bao-sheng (Jewel-Victorious) Bodhisattva:
Kumārajīva says that his jewel-like merit transcends the world.
Tian-wang (Heaven-King) Bodhisattva: Kumārajīva says—
First, the nominal Heavenly King, who is called "Heaven.
Second, the born devas, the various celestial beings.
Third, the noble sages and great beings (*mahāsattvas*), all of whom manifest in this life.
Bodhisattva Huaimo: Kumārajīva says, "One who practices the path that destroys Māra. Bodhisattva Diandei:
Kumārajīva says, [“One who attains [realization] like lightning.”]
The name is derived from his activity.

Guṇakāra-saṃdarśana Bodhisattva: Kumārajīva says, "The marks of merit adorn the body.
Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva: Kumārajīva says... [text fragment]
By means of the sound of the Great Dharma, he causes sentient beings to be subdued.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Thunder-Sound (Ghoṣeśvara), Kumārajīva said:

The multitude of evil ones tremble with fear, as if hearing the sound of thunder, causing those who hear it to feel both joy and dread.

"By means of the great Dharma-sound, one subdues the stubborn and fierce; the resonance vibrates and strikes like two mountains colliding."
Regarding the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, Kumārajīva said:

Aksobhya Bodhisattva; Kumārajīva says:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; Kumārajīva says: [Mañjuśrī].

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva— Śikṣānanda says:
When there are perils in the world, those who invoke his name and take refuge in the Bodhisattva are immediately liberated upon hearing his voice;
he is also named Avalokiteśvara (The One Who Observes the World’s Cries).
He is also named Avalokiteśvara.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Brahmajāla, Kumārajīva said:
The four Brahma-vihāras— loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—
are described by the Net as being numerous.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnadaṇḍa, Kumārajīva said:
Whether taking material treasures or the Dharma-treasure as a staff,
the Bodhisattva Unsurpassed excels with his transcendent merit.
Bodhisattva Adorned Land; Śikṣānanda says:
"Purifying the Buddha-land.
Bodhisattva Golden Topknot; Śikṣānanda says: [Purifying the Buddha-land].

He fully perceives the worlds of the ten directions, as well as the causes, conditions, karmic actions, and retributions of sentient beings.
Regarding "Maitreya Bodhisattva," Kumārajīva says that this is his clan name (*gotra*).
This is called Maitreya;
"Ajita" is its name,
which translates as "Unconquerable."
He was the son of a Brahmin from South India.
Mañjuśrī Dharmaputra Bodhisattva; Shi (Kumārajīva) says that in the language of Qin, this means "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode).

furthermore, because he comes to succeed the Buddha’s position, he is called a "Dharma Prince.
Such as these were thirty-two thousand people—this is the number of the assembly of the five groups.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand Brahma Kings, such as Śikhin and others, who came from other four-continent worlds to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma. Below this, three groups of miscellaneous assemblies are listed.
"This assembly of Brahma Kings.

In the language of Qin, this means "topknot.

Yakṣa. Zhaò says:

Gandharva; this is translated as "Fragrant Shade" (xiāngyìn). Zào says:

Asura. Zhaò says: In the Qin language, this means "those who do not drink wine.

The Nāga deity as well.

the eight precepts constitute the male lay practitioner observing the fast (*upavāsastha*)."
The *upāsikās* all came together to sit in the assembly; "yī" (夷) means "woman," which may be understood according to the preceding [explanation].

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded with reverence by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands as he preached the Dharma for them. These two [sections] clarify how the Buddha manifested supernatural transformations to startle beings and cause them to believe and take refuge, like a jewel of nocturnal light that does not require one to draw a sword to examine it.
How much more so for that which is profound and subtle!
To transmit it before one has faith in it—
among all things, this is easily followed.
It is difficult to comprehend through rational understanding;
therefore, divine transformation is manifested without fixed form to enable beings to receive and practice it.
This text is divided into two distinct parts.

First, the manifestation of the Buddha’s supreme body is clarified; subsequently, the offering of the parasol by Ratnakūṭa is explained. In the preceding text, there were three parts: the Dharma, the metaphor, and their synthesis.
This [section] constitutes the first part: the manifestation of the supreme body.
Previously, it was taught that the Dharma of the Hīnayāna is subtle and its manifestations inferior.
Now I shall explain how the Mahāyāna Dharma is superior and its characteristics are superior.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Clad in tattered, filthy garments and holding a refuse-removing vessel."
This indicates that he formerly manifested inferior signs for the sake of the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, it says:
"Within that gate, he sat upon a lion throne and arrayed precious objects."
This indicates that the Mahāyāna manifests superior characteristics. Therefore,
in the subsequent verses, the phrase "pure, cultivated, and broad" praises the superior characteristics of the teaching,
while "neither existent nor non-existent" praises the superior nature of the Dharma.
The passage beginning with "At the Bodhi tree" praises the inferior characteristics [of the Śrāvaka vehicle],
while the passage concerning the "three turnings of the wheel of Dharma" praises the provisional teachings.
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, manifesting itself within the great ocean.
He sits securely upon a lion throne made of various jewels, eclipsing the entire assembly of those who have gathered; this is like the metaphor of Mount Sumeru.
"Sits securely upon various jewels" and so forth refers to the union.
Zhaò said:
"Sumeru, in the language of Qin, means 'Wondrous High Mountain.
It stands in the midst of the great ocean, rising three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand li above the water."
The Tathāgata, standing amidst the fourfold assembly, was preeminent in his majestic appearance;
his radiance eclipsed the great multitude like a mountain of gold manifesting upon the vast ocean.
At that time, there was a son of a householder in the city of Vaiśālī.
His name was Ratnakūṭa.
Accompanied by five hundred sons of householders,
he came to where the Buddha was, carrying parasols made of the seven precious gems.

They prostrated with their heads at his feet, each offering a parasol together to the Buddha. These two lines clarify the presentation of the parasols and manifest the auspicious signs that symbolize the teaching on the Pure Land.
This section consists of three parts.
First, offer the canopy;
next, join the canopy;
finally, return the faith.
This first offering of the canopy symbolizes the great compassion that shelters all beings;
being born through transformation in the Pure Land is precisely the manifestation of this great compassion.
Zhaò said:
"Ratnakūṭa was also a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body,
who constantly accompanied Vimalakīrti in visiting the Tathāgata to jointly propagate the Way and its teachings."
Now, that he went alone with a fellow villager to visit the Buddha was intended to provide the occasion for inquiring after his illness and to open the gateway to this scripture.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all the precious canopies were miraculously joined together to form a single canopy.
It completely covers the trichiliocosm; these two lines together form the text on the canopy.
First is the canopy itself, which symbolizes that internal compassion is without objective conditions and transcends the duality of self and other.
The manifestation of external pure lands symbolizes the differentiation of responding to sentient beings, wherein the pure and the defiled are distinct;
this is the first point.
As long as "self" and "other" have not been extinguished, the assembly of Ratnakūṭa and others remains diverse, and their compassion remains limited by attachment.
"The reason why all Buddhas, being of one nature, unite to compassionately cover the three thousandfold world-system," Kumārajīva said,
"is that there are two purposes for manifesting these supernatural transformations."
First, by manifesting immeasurable supernatural transformations, one’s wisdom is necessarily profound.
Second, by offering what is most precious, such as the Jewel Accumulation, one will certainly obtain a fruit that is likewise precious.
That which is accomplished in future lives will surely be as wondrous and luminous as this; from small causes, great fruits arise.
Furthermore, the broad and long characteristics of this world all appear therein.

Moreover, within this trichiliocosm—the various Mount Sumerus, Snow Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, Fragrant Mountains, Jewel Mountains, Gold Mountains, Black Mountains, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains; the great oceans, rivers, streams, springs, and sources; as well as the sun, moon, and stars; and the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of all the honored deities—all appear within the precious canopy. This is the second [aspect]: the manifestation of external distinctions.
The previous joining of the covers already symbolized that the Dharmakāya’s impartial compassion covers all without distinction;
this present differentiation also symbolizes that the Nirmāṇakāya manifests various lands according to conditions, being neither uniform nor dual.
First, manifesting in this world-system;
second, manifesting in the ten directions.
Within this section, there are three parts.
First, the ten mountains represent the dwelling places of land-dwelling sentient beings;
second, the great oceans represent the dwelling places of aquatic beings;
third, the sun, moon, and so forth represent the dwelling places of those who reside in space.
However, because these three categories are all covered by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they are all manifested within the "coverings" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Zhaò said:
"The coverings are neither broad nor pervasive."
The lands of the eight directions are neither narrow nor do they fail to appear within the precious canopy;
furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions and their preaching of the Dharma also appear within the precious canopy—this is the second manifestation of the ten directions.
The Wu edition states:

"The adornments and purity of the Buddha-lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the Buddhas dwelling and preaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions, all appear within the precious canopy.
This clearly demonstrates that the manifestation of signs reveals the fundamental principle; this can be seen therein.
Zhaò said:
"In order to manifest that the excellence of the Buddha-lands varies and is not uniform,
he universally manifests those of the ten directions."
All these sons of elders had long since resolved their minds on the Way, yet they had not yet cultivated the Pure Land.
Desiring to gladden them in their spirit of providing offerings and to inspire their aspiration for the Pure Land,
[the Buddha] manifested it by means of their very canopy.
At that time, the entire assembly, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

With palms joined, they prostrated before the Buddha and gazed up at his venerable countenance, never for a moment averting their eyes—this is the manifestation of the three karmas of devotion through the three acts of beholding the auspicious signs.
Śrī said:
"Faith and delight arise within and manifest as signs without.
This is the case with the elder’s son Ratnākara."
He then spoke in verse before the Buddha. Regarding these three sections below that inquire about the sūtras:
they extol the virtues of the Buddha to inspire faith in sentient beings, thereby serving as the basis for initiating the inquiry.
Sengzhao said:
"Physical reverence is insufficient to express the mind;
therefore, one further praises and chants it."
There are thirty-six verses in all.
The prose commentary consists of four parts.
First is the praise of the superiority of the Mahāyāna.
Second, praising the inferiority of the Hīnayāna;
third, praising the manifestation of auspicious omens;
fourth, praising the merits of the Buddha’s three secrets.
The preceding text also consists of three parts:
first, two lines that collectively praise his internal virtues;
second, two lines that clarify his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The third is the praise of the teaching through the five aspects;
this is the first [of those].
"His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses"—these first four lines constitute the praise of his physical form.
Sengzhao said:
"Among the five senses and the hundred members of the body, the eyes are the most prominent. Because one beholds the countenance with them, he first extols the eyes.
In India, there is the blue lotus flower."
Its leaves are long and broad,
with a clear distinction between green and white;
because they possess the marks of a great man’s eyes, they are used as a metaphor for them.
"With a pure mind, he has already transcended all meditative concentrations"—this phrase praises the mind.
Zhaò says:
"As for 'his form is long'..."
Regarding the virtue of the Lord of the Eye:
when one praises the eye with the mind, it encompasses all appearances;
when one praises the mind, it encompasses all virtues.
Therefore, the author designates two [verses] as the opening of the hymn:
"The ocean of meditative concentration is deep and vast, without limit;
were it not for the Tathāgata’s pure true mind, none could cross it."
"Having long accumulated pure karma, his renown is immeasurable"—this phrase praises the cause.
Zhaò says:
"Because he accumulated the three types of pure karma throughout incalculable kalpas, his fame and name are immeasurable."
"Because you lead the multitude to tranquility, I bow my head"—this phrase praises the fruit [of enlightenment].
It means that you travel together with the multitude upon the Eightfold Noble Path to reach the tranquility of nirvāṇa;
therefore, I pay homage.
Zhaò said:
"Quiescence refers to the Way of unconditioned cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
Having seen the Great Sage manifest his spiritual transformations throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions,"
"Among them, the various Buddhas expound the Dharma;
all these are seen and heard. These two lines praise their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
This is because, through seeing, one perceives that the lands in the central regions differ in being either pure or defiled.
This is to provide the reason for sending inquiries to those below.
Zhaor said:
"Since the divine transformations of the joined canopy have already been seen, they are beyond measure."
Within that space, the lands of the ten directions and all Buddhas preaching the Dharma appeared;
thereupon, the entire assembly in this Sahā world saw and heard them from afar, which was a rare and marvelous occurrence.
The Dharma-king’s power of Dharma transcends all living beings;
he constantly bestows the wealth of Dharma upon all. This third section praises the act of preaching the Dharma.
This first part marks the gift of Dharma.
Zhaò said:
"A secular king, by virtue of his worldly power, can bestow benefits upon an entire nation;
a Dharma King, by virtue of the power of the Dharma, transcends the multitudes and is thus able to guide and deliver them boundlessly."
"Able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena,
yet remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth"— these two lines praise the meaning of the Dharma King.
Zhaò says:
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the meaning of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Although one may differentiate their diverse characteristics, this does not contradict the single characteristic.
This is the sublime path of the Dharma King; to deviate from it through superficiality is to err.
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, I therefore prostrate to this King of Dharma. ZHAO says:
"A worldly king possesses mastery over his subjects."
The Dharma King exercises mastery over the Dharma;
the Dharma has no fixed characteristics,
and it is excellent to explain it according to what is appropriate.
When there is difference, one distinguishes the differences without contradicting the sameness; this is excellence.
When there is sameness, one distinguishes the sameness without contradicting the differences.
Because the distinctions between sameness and difference are articulated such that both accord with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one attains mastery.
"The teaching of the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent. These three explanations praise the Mahāyāna doctrine of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) that has been taught.

Here, the first clarifies that because things exist through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are "existent yet not existent," which refers to the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma-śūnyatā*).
This differs from the Hīnayāna, which abandons existence to realize emptiness;
because it does not transcend emptiness itself, it is called "attachment to dharmas" (dharmagrāha).
Zhaò said:
If one wishes to say that existence exists, it does not arise of itself;
if one wishes to say that it is non-existent, it takes form through the convergence of conditions.
That this form arises through convergence does not mean it is nothingness.
It is not that non-existence is called existence;
because existence exists, there is non-existence.
If there were no existence, what non-existence could there be?
Because there is non-existence, there is existence;
if there were no non-existence, how could there be existence?
Thus, that which exists inherently does not exist.
"Because it is non-existent in itself, it is not non-existent.
This is the correct teaching of the Dharma King.
"All phenomena arise by way of causes and conditions" is the explanation of this statement.
Sengzhao said:
"Existence does not arise from conditions,
nor does non-existence arise from conditions."
Because phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, they arise from causes and conditions.
The treatise says:
Because phenomena arise from conditions, they do not exist [inherently].
Because it arises through conditions, it is not non-existent.
"There is no self, no agent, and no experiencer"—the following verse clarifies that the self is fundamentally non-existent;
thus, there is no "non-self," and one enters the gate of non-duality.
This differs from the two vehicles, which abandon the notion of self and abide in non-self.
Furthermore, "I create" and "I receive" are distinct names for the three types of conceiving a self.
This clarifies that the form is transmuted by means of karma.
How could there be a permanent self that presides over these diverse forms?
Zhaò said:
"All phenomena arise solely from conditions."
Because there is no separate true sovereign that presides over it, there is no self (*ātman*).
Since it is by virtue of having a self that one can perform good and evil deeds and receive calamity or fortune,
and since there is no self, there is neither one who performs nor one who receives.
"The karma of good and evil does not perish" is the explanation. Zhaò says:
"If there were neither an agent nor a recipient, then conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) would not exist."
One who well attains merit brings about calamity through evil.
Yet, the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings transmit beauty and ugliness;
because the way of retribution arises, they follow one another in a linked chain, just as sound accords with its echo and a straight form produces an upright shadow.
This is the natural principle;
it does not deviate by even a hair's breadth.
Why, then, should one further rely upon a permanent self to preside over it?

"Initially, beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power and attained the realization of the path to the extinction of ambrosia. These two sets of eight verses praise the past teaching of the Hīnayāna, wherein he manifested an inferior body as a provisional means to benefit sentient beings.
The text has four parts.
The first two lines clarify the attainment of the Way;
the second two lines clarify the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
The first two lines clarify the attainment of benefit;
the next two lines show the equality toward enemies and kin.
This initial radiance subdues Māra and realizes cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
That is to say, the Tathāgata left the royal palace, severed his attachments, and departed the city; he underwent trials on heterodox paths,
abandoned those heterodoxies to sit beneath the tree,
and vowed to attain bodhi.
The palace of Māra trembles; first, he subdues the greed for form through skillful means, and next, he overcomes his enemies.
Only when the external māras have dispersed does he realize nirvāṇa.
Amṛta is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
herein, the internal māras of fetters and habitual tendencies are forever extinguished.
The "Buddha-tree" refers to bodhi.
"Beginning" refers to the initial stage.
"Already without mind or intent, and without sensation or activity,
yet completely subduing all non-Buddhists"— this explains the subduing of outsiders.
One interpretation states:
In the past, when practicing the six perfections, meditative concentration, asceticism, and so forth,
the Bodhisattva had no intention of accepting those heterodox teachings.
It is merely to demonstrate that he is identical [to them] in his subduing of others.
Furthermore, Zhaò said:
"What is this so-called 'mind'?"
Defilement arises from existence.
What is the recipient?
Suffering and pleasure are the traces of practice; the sage’s profound true essence is quiescent and like empty space.
Although his mind universally illumines the myriad dharmas, his heart has never experienced suffering or pleasure.
He passes through these sūtras without grasping at objects;
he is eternally quiescent.
How could it be that the mind can receive it?
This is the state where the mind is submissive toward all things, yet there is nothing that does not submit to it.
To "receive" means to grasp with attachment.

"Turning the wheel of the Dharma thrice throughout the great trichiliocosm, that wheel is from the beginning eternally pure. These two lines clarify his arrival at the Deer Park to turn the wheel of the Dharma;
for as soon as he attained the Way, he transformed sentient beings.
Next, the two aspects of the Dharma-text are explained;
herein, the turning of the Dharma is first clarified.
The three turnings consist of the turning that demonstrates the characteristics, the turning that exhorts practice, and the turning that provides corroboration.
This means that first, the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths are revealed;
next, one is exhorted to practice these Four Noble Truths;
and finally, it is stated that "I have already attained realization," so as to inspire faith and acceptance.
The "trichiliocosm" (mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu) is the single sphere of transformation of a Buddha.
Zhaò said:
"The Wheel of Dharma is eternally pure, like empty space."
Although past and present differ and times shift with changing customs,
the sages transmit one another so that their Way remains unchanged.
That celestial beings and humans attain the Way serves as its testimony.
"The Three Jewels thus appeared in the world; these two vidyās have achieved their efficacy.
Zhaò said:
"At the time of the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma, [the Buddha was with] the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya."
Eighty thousand devas attained the Way.
This is the clear realization of the path of constant purity;
having thus perfected the Jewel-Wheel of the Dharma, he became a Buddha.
Once the Jewel of the Dharma had been turned and the five men had left the household life to attain the Way,
the Sangha-jewel may be said to have begun from that point.
The five were Kauṇḍinya, Mahānāman, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, and Vāṣpa.
Using this sublime Dharma to rescue all living beings,
once received, they never regress and remain eternally tranquil.
The Great King of Physicians delivers them from old age, sickness, death, and rebirth.
One should pay homage to the boundless ocean of the Dharma; this is the benefit of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
It means that by clearly severing the afflictions of both the paths of seeing and cultivation, one attains the benefit of *nirvāṇa*.
Sengzhao says:
As for those at the highest level among the ninety-six types of paths,
they are also able to sever the fetters and be reborn in the heavens of the formless realm;
however, because their path is not essential or true, they will eventually fall back into the three miserable realms.
The Buddha saves sentient beings of the three vehicles with the sublime Dharma of the Four Truths; yet there are those who,
having received it, fall back into the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore it is said:
"Once received, there is no regression;
having forever completed the unconditioned, one is eternally tranquil."
Furthermore, because he remedies the most grievous afflictions of birth,
old age, sickness, and death with the medicine of the Dharma, he is the supreme among the Kings of Physicians.
Thus, this Wheel of Dharma is profound, vast, and unfathomable.
The Dharma-ocean flows with moisture without limit; his virtue is boundless.
Unmoved by praise or blame, he is like Mount Sumeru. This fourth section praises impartiality and consists of three parts.
This first part concerns being unmoved by the eight winds.
Zhaò said:

"The winds of the eight worldly dharmas—gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and disparagement, suffering and pleasure—cannot move the Tathāgata, just as the four winds cannot move Mount Sumeru.
He remains equanimous toward the good and the evil; he is unmoved by these two opposites of compliance and resistance through his compassion."
Zhaò said:
"To have no sorrow when one's hand is severed and no joy when one's foot is held up—good and evil belong to others;
with compassionate coverage, there is no duality."
Furthermore, being in accord with the Dharma, contrary to the Dharma, and neither contrary nor in accord—this is the equanimity of the mind.
The activity of the mind is as equal as space.
Who, upon hearing of this "Jewel among Men," would not receive it with reverence? This concludes the third section of the commentary.
Zhaò said:
"In heaven it is the Treasure of Heaven;
among humans it is the Treasure of Humanity."
Since these jewels belong to humans and devas, how could they be the work of mere devas or humans? Thus, there are none who do not reverently receive them.
Now, I offer this small canopy to the World-Honored One;
within it, my trichiliocosm is manifested.
The palaces where the devas, nāgas, and spirits dwell,
as well as those of the gandharvas and yakṣas—
all that exists in the world is seen by them.
The One of Ten Powers has compassionately manifested this transformation.
Seeing this rarity, the multitude all praised the Buddha.
"Now I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms. These four lines below praise the three offerings of the parasol and so forth; specifically, they praise the offering of the subtle parasol.
"Appearing therein" refers to the manifestation of the canopy.
"The multitude beholds it" refers to the multitude’s collective admiration. Zhaò says:
"Weiwei" means small.
That which is venerated is most subtle, yet that which is perceived is most vast;
this is what is manifested through the Tathāgata’s compassion.
"The Ten Powers" is merely another designation for the Tathāgata.
The Great Sage, the Dharma King, to whom all turn;
those who contemplate the Buddha with a pure mind find nothing but joy.
Each beholds the World-Honored One standing before them.
"Then there are the supernormal powers and the unique qualities"—this section below is the fourth, praising the Buddha’s merit in benefiting sentient beings through his three secrets.
This first part concerns the secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*).
As the Dharma King’s compassionate grace causes the masses to long for him with devotion, and as their pure faith varies, the Buddha likewise responds accordingly.
Sengzhao said:
"The Dharmakāya responds universally and perfectly, like the single moon rising in the sky and its reflection appearing in a hundred waters;
it is not shared with those of the Two Vehicles."
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice;
sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind,
all saying that the World-Honored One speaks in their own language.
"This is the supernatural power of the unshared dharma. The following six lines praise the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the secret of speech.
Of these, the first two lines concern the two analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
[The Buddha] understands the various names of all phenomena according to their respective types, each being distinct.
This is the eloquence of Dharma.
All these refer to the World-Honored One’s matching of others’ speech and sounds; this is the eloquence of words.
The Buddha attains the languages of all sentient beings.
Regarding "dhāraṇī":
it is the word beyond words, which is not shared with those of the two vehicles.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single sound.
"Sentient beings each, according to their respective understandings, universally receive and practice [the teaching] to obtain its benefits.
This is the power of spiritual transformation, the unshared dharma. These two lines praise the eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
For ordinary beings, it demonstrates the meaning of cause and effect, good and evil;
for those of the Two Vehicles, it demonstrates the meaning of impermanence, quiescence, and so forth;
for those of the Mahāyāna, it demonstrates the meaning of the true mark that is neither born nor extinguished.
Zhaò said:
"Those who delight in giving hear of giving;
those who delight in the precepts hear of the precepts."
Each experiences different sensations and performs different actions,
thereby obtaining their respective distinct benefits;
or rather, the pleasures of humans and devas are distinct.
Whether it be the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles or ultimate bodhi,
though moistened by the same single rain, the three types of grasses are not the same;
how could they be shared with the two vehicles?
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice,
some feel fear, some rejoice,
some give rise to weary detachment, and some sever their doubts.
"This, then, is the power of spiritual transformation, a quality not shared [with others]"; these two lines concern the eloquence of joyful exposition.
Zhaò said:
"When sentient beings hear of the retribution of suffering, they become terrified."
Hearing of the sublime fruit, one rejoices;
hearing of impurity, one feels weary and detached;
hearing the phenomena and their characteristics, one severs doubt.
I do not know what is being expounded by this single sound that causes ordinary beings to feel both joy and fear;
how could this possibly be shared by those of the Two Vehicles?
I prostrate to the One of Ten Powers, the Greatly Diligent.
I prostrate to those who have already attained fearlessness;
I prostrate to those who abide in the unshared dharmas;
I prostrate to all the Great Teachers of the Path. Below this, the seven lines constitute the third section, which praises the secret of the mind.
The first two verses praise the virtue of wisdom;
these two verses clarify the virtue of abandonment;
and the final three verses clarify the virtue of grace.
Wisdom merges with principle such that their aspects are identical and the mind is tranquil; it cannot be known through deliberation.
Its eloquence cannot be fixed by names or numbers, nor can it be expressed in words.
As for the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth:
This is merely a provisional means for instructing beings;
wisdom cannot be bent by force.
To have no fear of external difficulties is what is meant by "fearlessness."
This is not shared with the two vehicles;
its categories and enumerations are as detailed elsewhere.
I prostrate to the one who can sever all fetters and bonds.
"I prostrate to those who have already reached the other shore. The following section consists of verses praising his virtues.
While the followers of the Two Vehicles sever [their own afflictions] for themselves, the Great Sage both severs them and delivers others.
This first [stage] involves severing the fetters for oneself.
"Fetters" refers to the nine fetters:
the five dull afflictions (mūla-kleśa), namely craving, aversion, pride, ignorance, and doubt.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) consists of the three views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*). The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) consists of the view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
These two fetters comprise the five deluded proclivities (*pañca-kleśa-nīvaraṇa*).
The fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) are two among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

As for the bonds (*bandhana*), there are four: the bond of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-bandhana*), the bond of ill will (*vyāpāda-bandhana*), the bond of attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-bandhana*), and the bond of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-bandhana*).
It is also said:
The three fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion— furthermore,
when a single thought grasps at signs and suddenly becomes deluded regarding ultimate truth, all the myriad afflictions that arise from this are termed "bonds.
Thus, all afflictions are called "fetters" (saṃyojana).
All these are called "bonds.
I prostrate to the one who can deliver all the worlds;
I prostrate to the one who has forever left the path of birth and death. This clarifies the liberation from one's own fetters.
He is thus able to deliver all the world from birth and death.
He fully knows the characteristics of the coming and going of sentient beings and is skillful in attaining liberation through all phenomena.
The following section clarifies the third point: transformation through unconditioned compassion, which constitutes his benevolent virtue.
This practice knows that beings come and go, yet remains unattached to phenomena.
Zhaò says:
"Sentient beings travel back and forth through the six realms of existence, their minds galloping about."
It is not that one knows all things as they are.
Furthermore, because I am defiled by various dharmas, those dharmas bind me;
if my mind were free from defilement, then all fetters would be liberated.

Unattached to the world like a lotus flower, he constantly and skillfully enters the practice of emptiness and stillness; through this practice, he knows the world is like an illusion, yet his great compassion does not abandon it.
Zhaò says:
Entering and exiting with mastery, yet not deviating from tranquility, he constantly enters [the state of meditative absorption] with skill.

Penetrating the characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction, I bow my head to him who is like space, having no dependence. This practice clarifies that one understands all phenomena without grasping or attachment.
Sengzhao said:
"The myriad dharmas are profound and mysterious; who can discern their origins?
Only the Buddha, being unimpeded, alone is called 'thoroughly penetrating. Yet the Sage’s mind has no point of attachment, just as space has no support."
At that time, the elder’s son Ratnākara,
having spoken these verses, addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, these five hundred sons of elders..."
"All have already resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Below this, the main body (*śarīra*) is clarified.
Since the preceding introductory section (*nidāna*) has already served to strike the heart with wonder, offer praise, inspire faith, and provoke resolution, [the main body now follows].
This section consists of three parts concerning the attainment of realization, the fruit of enlightenment, and the benefits gained through the direct inspiration of the faculties.
First, from the beginning up to the middle of the "Buddha-land" chapter, the Dharma King proclaims the fundamental tenets.
Second, from the "Expedient Means" chapter downward through nine subsequent chapters, the Great Beings assist the Buddha in propagating his transformational teachings.
The three bodhisattva practices, having completed the proclamation of the two chapters on beholding Akṣobhya, return to the seal of stabilization.
This is like a king proclaiming a righteous edict, which the ministers carry out; once the affairs are concluded, they return to pay court to their sovereign.
The first section has two parts:
first, Ratnakūṭa’s request for the teaching;
second, the Tathāgata’s response.
The first part of the introductory petition has two sections.
The first clarifies that the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) constitutes the very faculty capable of hearing the Dharma.
Zhaò says:
*Anuttara* in the language of Qin means "unsurpassed"; *samyak-saṃbodhi* in the language of Qin means "right and universal knowledge.
