In the Mahāyāna, because one knows that dharmas are like illusions, there is neither arising nor ceasing, and thus one enters non-duality.
Zhaò says:
"Ceasing" merely refers to the ceasing of arising.
"If one awakens to the absence of arising and ceasing, what is there to be extinguished?
This is precisely the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because this bodhisattva realized the Way by contemplating arising and ceasing, he spoke of his own understanding as the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
The following passage displays the clouds of the ten thousand dharmas:
since everything apart from the truth is termed "duality," it is therefore spoken of as "non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Guṇarakṣita said:
"Self and what belongs to self constitute duality.
Because there is a self, there is that which belongs to self."
If there is no self, then there is no "mine.
This is entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"The wondrous master is the eternally abiding self."
The body and the myriad things are "mine" (*mama*);
"mine" refers to that which belongs to the self.
Since phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of self, who is there to possess them?
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said:
"To accept and not to accept constitute a duality.
If one does not accept any phenomenon, it cannot be apprehended."
Because they cannot be apprehended, there is no grasping and no relinquishing, no action and no practice;
this is entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas. Ordinary beings accept and cling to the five aggregates, whereas those beyond training do not accept them.
This is the second point.
Zhaò said:
"Where there is a mind, there must be that which is received."
To accept something while necessarily refusing another constitutes duality.
If one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and neither accepts nor refuses, then there is neither attainment nor action; this is non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Śīrṣaka said:
"Defilement and purity are two.
To see the true nature of defilement is to have no mark of purity; this accords with the mark of my extinction."
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Ordinary beings, with their inverted minds, perceive impurity;
those of the Three Vehicles contemplate the body as impure.
These constitute duality.
Zhaò says:
Purity arises from defilement;
in the true nature, there is neither defilement nor purity.
"What is purity?
The Bodhisattva Sunakṣatra replied,
"To say 'this is movement' and 'this is thought' constitutes duality."
When there is no movement, there is no thought;
when there is no thought, there is no discrimination.
One who thoroughly penetrates this—
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"The arousal of emotion constitutes movement; the formation of conceptualization constitutes thought.
Furthermore, he explains:
To abide securely in the true nature is for that nature to be immovable;
to be immovable is to be without thought.
The Bodhisattva Good Eye said:
The single characteristic and the absence of characteristics constitute two.
If one knows that the single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics,
one does not even grasp at the absence of characteristics, but enters into equanimity.

This is what is meant by "entering the gate of non-dual dharmas. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the one true reality (*ekābhāva-lakṣaṇa*), while the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies signlessness (*animitta*).
Sengzhao says:
To speak of "one" is to eliminate duality; it does not mean to cling to one.
To speak of "non-existence" is to eliminate existence; it does not mean to cling to non-existence.
Yet those who are deluded, upon hearing of "one," grasp at the characteristic of one.
Because one perceives non-existence, one grasps at the signless; thus there are two.
The Bodhisattva Subāhu said:
The bodhisattva-mind and the śrāvaka-mind constitute two.
One who contemplates that the characteristics of the mind are empty and like an illusion has neither bodhisattva-mind nor śrāvaka-mind.
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Kumārajīva said:
"Because of the merit from his giving, his hands produce inexhaustible precious objects;
because they are like the five rivers, he is named Subāhu (Wondrous Arm)."
Another interpretation states:
the mind of the śrāvaka is for self-benefit;
the mind of the bodhisattva is for the benefit of others.
The Bodhisattva Puṣya said:
"Good and not-good constitute duality;
if one does not give rise to good or not-good,"
To enter the limit of signlessness and attain thorough penetration—this is what it means to enter the gateway of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"Puṣya is the name of a lunar mansion."
Kumārajīva said:
"He was named after the causes encountered at the time of his birth;
'not good' refers to the ten non-virtuous actions."
"The ten wholesome paths and nirvana.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda said:
"Transgression and merit constitute duality."
If one realizes that the nature of sin is no different from merit,
and through diamond-like wisdom comprehends these marks such that there is neither bondage nor liberation,
this is entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas. "Sin" refers to the breaking of precepts.
Merit consists of precept, concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
That merit and demerit are equal, being of one mark and one nature, constitutes non-duality.
Zhaò said:
"Vajramati is the wisdom of the true mark.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said,
"The outflowing and the non-outflowing constitute a duality."
If one realizes the equality of all dharmas, then one does not give rise to the notion of outflows or the notion of being without outflows;
one does not cling to signs, nor does one dwell in signlessness.
This is called entering the gate of non-duality. Suffering, its origin, that which has outflows, and cessation are dual; the path and that which is without outflows are dual.
The Mahāsattva contemplates with equanimity that the single ultimate truth is non-dual.
Kumārajīva said:
"When a lion crosses water, it must cut straight across the current."
"Deviousness means lacking measure.
This Great Being, by means of the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), has deeply penetrated all phenomena and directly crossed to the other shore;
therefore, he is given this name by way of metaphor.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhivimukti said:
"Conditioned and unconditioned constitute a duality.
If one is free from all numerical reckoning, then the mind is like space."
To possess pure wisdom that is unimpeded is the entry into the gate of non-duality. The four marks are conditioned;
the cessation of the four marks is unconditioned.
The marks are fundamentally non-arising;
now they are neither extinguished nor dualistic.
Ruyi said:
"Number" refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said:
"The mundane and the supramundane constitute duality."
That the emptiness of worldly nature is itself the supramundane—
neither entering nor exiting it, neither overflowing nor dispersing therein—
is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Kumārajīva said:
The mundane refers to the three realms;
the supramundane refers to liberation.
Because one awakens to the nature of the world as eternally abiding, without entering or exiting, they are non-dual.
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣita said:
"Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa constitute a duality.
If one perceives the nature of birth-and-death, then there is no birth-and-death."
There is neither bondage nor liberation, neither burning nor extinction.
To understand it thus is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma; this is what is meant by undergoing birth and death in future existences.
When subsequent existence is extinguished, there is nirvana.
To awaken to the birth-and-death of the world is to realize that, in reality, there is no birth-and-death.
Zhaò said:
Bondage is indeed birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
death and separation are termed liberation and extinction (*nirvāṇa*), which are alternative designations for it.
The Bodhisattva Pratyakṣadarśin said:
"Exhaustion and non-exhaustion constitute duality.
If a phenomenon is ultimately exhausted or not exhausted, it possesses the characteristic of inexhaustibility."
The characteristic of inexhaustibility is itself emptiness;
in emptiness, there is neither the characteristic of exhaustion nor the characteristic of non-exhaustion.
One who enters in this manner—
This is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
Conditioned dharmas are deceptive and impermanent, and are therefore called "exhausted.
The true mark (*dharmatā*) is unconditioned and eternally abiding, and is therefore not exhausted.
If one regards exhaustion as exhaustion and non-exhaustion as non-exhaustion, both are dualistic.
If one can awaken to the fact that both exhaustion and non-exhaustion are devoid of the characteristic of exhaustion,
then one enters the gate of emptiness, which is non-dual.
The Bodhisattva Universal Guard said:
"Self and non-self constitute a duality.
Since even 'self' cannot be apprehended, how could 'non-self' be apprehended?"
One who perceives my true nature no longer gives rise to duality;
this is entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas. Zhaò says:
"Non-self arises from self."
"One who perceives my true nature finds that 'I' am fundamentally non-existent;
how much more so, then, that which is not-I?
The Bodhisattva Vidyutdeva said:
Knowledge and ignorance are two.
The true nature of ignorance is itself knowledge;
knowledge, moreover, cannot be grasped and is beyond all numerical categories.
To be equanimous and non-dual therein is the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"This clarifies that wisdom is illumination."
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusive darkness.
To see the nature of ignorance is itself illumination.
If one sees illumination as illumination, then that illumination is merely relative to ignorance; therefore, it cannot be grasped.
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"To regard form and emptiness as two is dualistic.
Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases to exist for there to be emptiness, but rather the very nature of form is itself empty."
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the emptiness of consciousness, constitute a duality.
Consciousness itself is emptiness; it is not that consciousness ceases to be empty, for the very nature of consciousness is itself empty.
One who penetrates this [reality] therein—
This is entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality: form is obstruction;
the cessation of form is emptiness—these are two.
If one realizes that the nature of form is itself empty, [there is no duality].
This is precisely the non-duality of emptiness and form.
Zhaò says:
"If there were something that did not immediately coincide with emptiness, there would be no leveling of its traces."
The other aggregates may be understood by analogy.
The Bodhisattva Mingxiang said:
"The four elements and the element of space constitute two distinct categories."
The four kinds of natures are themselves the nature of emptiness.
Just as the prior limit and the posterior limit are empty, so too is the middle limit empty.
One who can thus know all natures—
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"The four kinds are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The element of space is the great element of emptiness."
These five aggregates arise from this, and therefore it is called the "seed.
Furthermore, the abiding of these four great elements—being without before, after, or middle, and without distinction—is the element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*).
Another interpretation is as follows:
In the Hīnayāna, the four great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—are considered distinct from the element of space.
In the Mahāyāna *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, however, the four great elements are regarded as mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*);
because their nature is illusory and lacks intrinsic existence (*svabhāva*), they are not distinct from space.
The Bodhisattva Subhamati said:
"The eye and forms constitute a duality.
If one knows the nature of the eye such that it is neither greedy for, nor angry toward, nor deluded by forms, [then there is no duality]."
This is called tranquility.
Likewise, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena constitute duality.
If one knows the nature of the mind such that it is without greed, hatred, or delusion regarding mental phenomena, [this is non-duality].
This is called quiescence.
To dwell securely within it is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas. Zhaò says:
Because one acts upon the objects of the sensory passions, the three poisons arise.
"If one awakens to the nature of the six sense-faculties, then poison does not arise;
this is the path of quiescent extinction.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
To dedicate the gift toward omniscience is duality.
The very nature of the gift is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience.
It is the same for ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
To dedicate toward omniscience is duality.
The nature of wisdom is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience.
To enter into the single characteristic within this is [non-duality].
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"The six perfections are the wondrous cause;
dedicating them toward omniscience is the second."
If one awakens to the fact that cause and effect share the same nature and enters into the single characteristic,
then one accords with non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Profound Wisdom said:
To regard emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as two is dualistic.
Emptiness is itself signlessness, and signlessness is itself wishlessness.
If there is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, then there is no mind, thought, or consciousness.
That one gate of liberation is itself the three gates of liberation—this is the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The Śrāvaka sūtras clarify the three samādhis as having the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths as their object; the Mahāyāna takes the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as its causal condition."
This means that because the truths (satya) differ in the Hīnayāna, the gateways of samādhi differ;
whereas because the principle is the same in the Mahāyāna, the gateways of samādhi do not differ.
Zhaò said:
Although the three modes of practice differ, they are all equally liberation without objective conditions; therefore, there is no mind, thought, or consciousness.
Since the conditions are identical, the three liberations are not distinct.
The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said:
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha constitute a duality.
The Buddha is itself the Dharma;
the Dharma is itself the Sangha.
These Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned and are equal to space;
all phenomena are likewise so.
One who can practice in accordance with this—
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality: it is the Buddha of the sixteen-foot body;
it is the Dharma of the Four Truths;
and it is the Sangha of the fruits of the four paths.
This refers to the differences in the realization of the traces [of the path] within the Hīnayāna.
Wisdom is the Buddha of non-arising;
principle is the Dharma of signlessness.
The practice of non-cultivation is the Sangha.
This is because the fundamental principle of the Mahāyāna is one;
it is only because the Hīnayāna clings to traces that they appear different.
The Mahāyāna returns to the source and is therefore not different.
That the mind is unimpeded is the Bodhisattva’s greatness;
that the body exists and that the body is extinguished constitute duality.
The body is itself the cessation of the body.
Why is this? Because one who perceives the true reality of the body does not give rise to the view of a body or the view of its cessation.
The body and the cessation of the body are non-dual and without distinction;
to be neither startled nor afraid within this is to enter the gateway of the non-dual Dharma.
The aggregates are a mass of suffering, and the body is the locus of affliction and pain.
Therefore, the extinction of the body constitutes duality.
If one awakens to the fact that the aggregates are a provisional assembly, then the body is not a body, being without arising or extinction;
this is called seeing the true reality as non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Shangshan said:
"The actions of body, speech, and mind constitute duality.
These three types of action are all characterized by non-action."
The mark of non-action of the body is the mark of non-action of speech;
the mark of non-action of speech is the mark of non-action of the mind.
These three marks of non-action of the karmas are the mark of non-action of all dharmas.
One who can thus conform to non-conceptual wisdom (anabhisaṃskāra-prajñā) enters the gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"Although the three karmas differ, their non-conceptual nature is one."
“The arising of all phenomena is rooted in the three karmas.
Since the three karmas do not exist, who creates all phenomena?
The Bodhisattva Futián replied:
Wholesome conduct, unwholesome conduct, and immovable conduct constitute two [categories].
The true nature of these three types of conduct is emptiness.
Being empty, there is no wholesome conduct, no unwholesome conduct, and no immovable conduct.
To not give rise to these three types of action is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas. Zhaò says:
"Merit refers to wholesome actions within the desire realm; 'sin' refers to the category of the ten unwholesome paths of action."
One does not cultivate the practices of the form or formless realms.
Furthermore, it is explained that false movement constitutes "practice" (saṃskāra).
When free from movement, there is equanimity.
The Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka said:
"To give rise to duality from the self constitutes duality."
One who perceives the true reality of me does not give rise to dualistic dharmas.
If one does not abide in dualistic dharmas, then there is no consciousness.
That which has nothing to cognize—
This is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality. Because of the grasping at a self, that which is confronted becomes dual.
Zhaò says: "Because of the self, there is the other."
The second name arises from this cause.
If one perceives the true mark of the self, then the consciousness of "self" and "other" has no basis to arise.
Bodhisattva Guṇagañja said:
To have the mark of something attained is duality.
If there is nothing attained, then there is neither grasping nor rejecting.
One who neither grasps nor rejects—
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"Attainment lies in the mark of self; it lies in 'self' and 'other. When the marks of attainment do not exist, who can grasp and who can abandon?"
Furthermore, another interpretation is that regarding phenomena, there is duality in the attainment of something that depends upon an object;
if there is nothing to be attained, then there is no duality.
The Bodhisattva Candrottara said:
"Darkness and light constitute a duality.
Where there is neither darkness nor light, there is no duality."
Why is this so? Just as consciousness is empty, without darkness, and without light when one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling,
the characteristics of all phenomena are likewise thus.
To be equanimous within this is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma. Zhaò says:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles enter the meditative absorption of cessation, wherein the six sense faculties are entirely extinguished."
"Though it passes through day and night, one does not perceive the difference between darkness and light.
This serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva having no mind regarding brightness or obscurity.
The Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal-Hand said:
To delight in nirvana and not to delight in the world constitutes duality.
If one does not delight in nirvana and does not feel aversion toward the world, then there is no duality. Why is this so?
If there is bondage, then there is liberation.
If there were fundamentally no bondage, who would seek liberation?
Where there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither delight nor aversion.
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Zhaò says:
"If the world is without bondage, why should one feel weary of it?
If nirvāṇa is without liberation, why should one take pleasure in it?"
The Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍarāja said:
"The right path and the wrong path constitute a duality.
One who abides in the right path does not discriminate between what is wrong and what is right."
To be free from these two is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas. Right and wrong paths constitute duality;
if one abides in the equality of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) without discrimination, this is called non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Real-Bliss said:
"Reality and unreality constitute a duality.
For one who perceives reality, even the highest does not perceive reality; how then could a mantra not be real?"
Why is this? It is not seen by the fleshly eye; only the eye of wisdom can see it.
And yet, this eye of wisdom neither sees nor does not see.
This is called entering the gate of non-dual dharmas. Zhaò says:
"The realm of the eye of wisdom of true reality is not what the physical eye can see.
Since the eye of wisdom does not perceive even 'reality' above all else, how much less could it perceive 'non-reality'?"
"Though it is said that there is no seeing, there is nothing that is not seen;
this is the essence of the eye of wisdom.
After each of these bodhisattvas had thus spoken, [the assembly remained silent].
Question: Mañjuśrī, what is the bodhisattva’s entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality?
This is the first question, and Mañjuśrī speaks in response.
Mañjuśrī said,
"As it appears to my mind,
regarding all phenomena, there is neither speech nor discourse."
"Without demonstration and without cognition, transcending all questioning and answering—this is the entry into the gate of non-duality.
This is the answer. Zhaò says:
Although the explanations provided by the various masters above are identical in their conclusion, their underlying reasons differ.
While they have directly analyzed the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they did not clarify the state beyond words.
Now, Mañjuśrī synthesizes the teachings of these various schools to open the gate of non-duality (*advaya*).
To state directly that the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are ineffable,
yet not to fail to employ words regarding these characteristics—
this statement is the ultimate of all speech.
Yet even as he remained in silent stillness, [the time] was still later.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"We have each spoken for ourselves;
now, O worthy one, you should speak.
What is this 'entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality'? This concludes the third section on Vimalakīrti’s discourse.
First, the question;
second, the answer;
third, the expression of approval.
This is the first [response].
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. This is the second response.
Zhaò said:
There is that which speaks of the unspeakable; yet,
if one remains unspeaking regarding the unspeakable,
that is why one maintains silence.
The aforementioned bodhisattvas expressed themselves through the characteristics of dharmas;
Mañjuśrī spoke through the ineffable;
and Vimalakīrti remained silent within the ineffable.
Although the essence of these three types of *vidyā* is the same, their manifestations differ in depth.
Thus it is said that one knows "subsequent non-knowing" through "subsequent wordlessness.
Mañjuśrī sighed and said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Even to the point where there are no words or speech—this is the direct entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. (This is the third exclamation.)
Zhaò said:
"The one who silently comprehends is Mañjuśrī;
it is because he awaits words that [the Buddha] praises him as excellent."
Dongsheng said:
"Since words and traces are exhausted in the wordless, it is praised as being true.
This was said when the 'Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Door of Non-Duality' was expounded."

Within this assembly, five thousand bodhisattvas all entered the gate of non-duality and attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas. This concludes the second part, clarifying how the assembly at that time obtained benefit.

Chapter Ten: The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation. This chapter, titled "The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation," concerns the arrival of the Nameless One who, following conditions, manifests through the cultivation of conditions to accord with the True Dharma that is signless. It takes as its title the appearance of conditions in accordance with these manifestations. Chapter Ten: The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation. The arrival of the Nameless One follows conditions to manifest through the cultivation of conditions, thereby accords with the True Dharma which is without marks.
Taking the appearance of conditions in accordance with these marks as the basis for the title of this chapter.
This is the fragrance of the traces of the Dharma-body’s precepts, meditative concentration, and so forth, manifesting in the lands to transform sentient beings.
Thereupon, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The time for the meal is approaching."
"Where should these sons of heaven and bodhisattvas eat? These two—purity and defilement—move together, clarifying the function of the Middle Way.
While the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni and that of Gandhavyūha are equal, their manifestations differ according to the conditions of sentient beings; thus, purity and defilement appear distinct.
This chapter has three sections:
first, the provisional reliance on mindfulness of food;
second, the mutual wandering between the pure and the defiled.
Third, the benefits gained from hearing the chapter.
The initial text has three parts;
first, the recollection.
Next comes the censure,
followed by the granting of permission;
this is the first thought-moment.
Kumārajīva said:
"There are three reasons why Śāriputra alone conceived this thought.
First, the substance of his karmic bondage has not yet reached the state of being without dependence."
Second, having severed worldly intent, he delights in the Great Dharma and remains unstained by it.
Third, he reflects upon his own state of dependence and realizes that the assembly is likewise;
thus, being at the head of the disciples, he ought to provide offerings for the multitude.
At that time, Vimalakīrti,
knowing his thoughts, spoke to him, saying:
"The Buddha has taught the eight liberations."
"Virtuous one, you have accepted and practiced [the teaching].
How could you listen to the Dharma while mixed with the desire for food? This is the second reprimand.
The joy of the eight liberations and meditative concentrations is the food that nourishes the Dharma-body.
Diverse desires and material food nourish the body of a venomous serpent.
Most people, for the sake of sustaining this poisonous body, neglect the cultivation of the Dharma-body.
Therefore, one should use mindfulness as a warning against this.
"If you wish to eat, wait but a moment;
I shall cause you to obtain food such as you have never experienced before. This was the third permission.
In the Hīnayāna, one takes the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as the food of the Dharma.
Taking the five desires and solid food as poisonous sustenance,
the fact that one can now attain the Way through the meal of the Fragrant Accumulation is truly unprecedented.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi. This is the second section, "Mutual Travel between the Pure and the Impure.
It has three parts:
first, clarifying the mutual transformation of the two dharmas.
Second, it clarifies that the Buddha-activities of the two lands differ;
third, it clarifies the relinquishing of the defiled and rebirth in the pure.
In the first section, there are two parts.
First, it clarifies traveling from the defiled to the pure;
second, it clarifies coming from that purity to the defiled.
Within the preceding section, there are three parts.
First, the manifestation of the pure land;
second, the seeking of those who would go there;
third, the manifestation of the transformation-body going there.
The first section has three parts.
This begins with entering samādhi.
Yuì says that *samādhi* is "rectifying the mind" in the language of Qin.
There are two kinds:
first, those acquired through cultivation;
second, those obtained as retribution.
In samādhi, there is entirely no such thing as the names of entering, exiting, or remaining;
how much less so for the Dharma-body?
Now, when one speaks of "entering," is this not merely the manifestation of its traces?
By means of his supernormal powers, he manifested to the great assembly that in the region above,
beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers,
there was a land named Saṃghagandha.
The Buddha there is named Gandhottama-kūṭa.
He currently resides in that land, where the fragrance is the most supreme among the scents of humans and devas in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
In that realm, even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist.
There was only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas,
for whom the Buddha preached the Dharma;
the entire realm consisted entirely of pavilions made of fragrance.
The walking paths, the fragrant grounds, and the gardens were all perfumed;
the aroma of the food circulated throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
At that time, the Buddha was seated together with the bodhisattvas, about to partake of the meal.
There were devaputras, all named Gandhavatī,
who had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made offerings to that Buddha and the various bodhisattvas; these two manifested the pure land of Universal Fragrance.
The names such as "Fragrant Accumulation" indicate the purity of both the primary and secondary environments.
There is no retinue of followers belonging to the Two Vehicles;
the secondary environment consists of pavilions made of pure fragrance, and the Buddha-activities consist of pure seating and pure eating.
All in this great assembly have witnessed it with their own eyes; the multitude possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge has seen it as well.
May they behold these sublime signs and give rise to faith, so that when the meal is served, they may look forward to the Way.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"O virtuous ones, who among you is able to bring back the meal from that Buddha? These two [questions] regarding those seeking to go consist of four phrases."
This was the first instance of seeking to go there.
Zhaò said:
"Having manifested in that land, he sought out those with power and ordered them to fetch the food."
By the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, everyone remained silent. [The commentary states: "Two spiritual powers caused them to be silent.
ZHAO says:
Mañjuśrī, intending to manifest the virtue of Vimalakīrti, used his spiritual power to cause the assembly to remain silent."
Vimalakīrti said, "O worthy one, this great assembly would surely find this shameful. He rebuked him three times.
Zhaò said:
The encouragement of those who have not yet attained perfection. Mañjuśrī said:
"As the Buddha has said, do not disparage those who have not yet studied. (4) The citation of the response.
Zhaò said:
"Jìn" refers to the beginning of study.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti—

Without rising from his seat, he manifested before the assembly a bodhisattva whose physical marks, minor characteristics, radiance, and majestic power were so preeminent that they eclipsed the entire assembly. Hereafter, three points clarify the manifestation and departure.
The text has three parts:
first, departing for the transformation [of beings];
second, inquiring after [the Buddha’s] well-being.
The three assemblies offered praise.
In the first section of the text, there are four parts;
this is the first, which manifests a transformation to send [the messenger] forth.
The reason for manifesting these transformations before the assembly was to cause them to behold the superior manifestations and thereby seek their origin.
He then addressed them, saying:
"Go to the realm above."
The distance between the divisions was equal to forty-two Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands.
There was a land named Saugandhika;
the Buddha there was named Gandhottama.
He was sitting and eating together with various bodhisattvas. Second, this indicates the destination:
"Go there and speak on my behalf, saying:
'Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One.'"

I pay my respects and inquire after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness or affliction and whether your physical strength remains secure. This is the inquiry according to the Three Teachings.
Zhaò says:
"This is offered to show that one who possesses a body cannot be without suffering; therefore, this inquiry is made."
The Tathāgata has still said that he has little illness and little affliction;
we pray that you might grant us the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal,
so that we may perform the work of the Buddha within the Sahā world.
It causes those who delight in minor dharmas to attain the vast Great Way, and it also causes the fame of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere. "Fourfold entreaty for a meal" (sìchénqǐngfàn):
Zào says this consists of further humble and deferential words.
In that land, the Great Way is realized through fragrance;
because the beings of this country are narrow-minded and inferior in their aspirations, they requested the remains of the fragrant food to propagate the Buddha’s work.
Thereupon, the transformed bodhisattva immediately ascended to the upper regions before the assembly.

The entire assembly saw him go to the World of Fragrant Flowers (*Gandhavatī*) and prostrate at the feet of that Buddha. This section on the two emanations arriving to inquire after his health has three parts;
this is the first:
the arrival of the emanation and the prostration at the feet.
Furthermore, I heard these words:
"Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One.

He pays infinite respects and inquires after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your physical strength is secure. These two inquiries concern one's well-being.
I pray that I may obtain the remnants of the World-Honored One’s meal,
desiring to perform Buddha-work within the Sahā world,
so that those who delight in inferior teachings may attain the Great Way.
They also caused the fame of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere; these three points describe the matters of their request exactly as in the text.
Those great beings, seeing the manifested bodhisattva, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
"From where has this superior person come?
Where is the Sahā world located?
And why is one called a 'follower of the lesser Dharma'?"
He immediately questioned the Buddha. The following section clarifies the three ways in which that Great Being was struck with wonder;
it consists of four parts, of which this is the first: the question of praise.
The inquiry consists of three parts.
First, asking from where [it] comes;
one should say it comes from that which has been emanated by whom.
This is a transformation created by Vimalakīrti.
Second, he asks about the Sahā world;
"Sahā" means "the place of manifold assemblies."
Sentient beings of various evil natures gather together in one place;
it is also called "Endurance" (Sahā).
Only the Buddha Śākyamuni is capable of enduring [such questions].
Regarding the third question, "Who are those who delight in inferior teachings?
Zhaò says:
Because that land is purely of the Mahāyāna and the name of those who delight in the Lesser Dharma is not heard there, he asks this question.
The Buddha told him:
"Below this world, past as many buddha-lands as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers..."
There is a world named Sahā.
The Buddha there is titled Śākyamuni.
He currently resides in this world of the five turbidities and evil.
For the sake of sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings,
he expounds the Way and its doctrines. There is a bodhisattva there named Vimalakīrti,
who dwells in the inconceivable liberation.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas;

therefore, he has dispatched these emanations to extol my name and praise this land, so as to cause those bodhisattvas to increase their merit and virtue. These two [points] answer the three questions.
With forty-two *gaṅgā-vālukā* [eons], he answered the second question regarding the place of origin.
With "presently in the five turbidities" (*pañca-kaṣāya*), he answered the third question.
By stating the reason for his small stature and mentioning the bodhisattva named Vimalakīrti, he answered the first question in reverse order.
The one who can transform is Śākyamuni;
this is translated as "Capable Nature.
Muni is translated as "Silent Name" (or "Sage").
That bodhisattva said:
"What kind of person is he that can perform such transformations?
His power of merit, his fearlessness, and his supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) are such as these. He asked this three times.
Having witnessed the majesty of the transformative deeds and the wondrous power of the light’s ability to manifest transformations, he asked again.
The Buddha said:
It is exceedingly great.
He dispatches emanations throughout all the ten directions to perform Buddha-works and benefit sentient beings.
This is the fourth response, intended to inspire longing and cause them to come to this Sahā world.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa filled a bowl of various fragrances with fragrant food and gave it to the transformed bodhisattvas. From here below, the second section clarifies the journey from the pure land to the defiled realm;
this passage consists of three parts.
First, receiving the rice together with those who have come;
second, the Pure Name guest awaits;
third, the meal constitutes a Buddhist service.
The first section of the middle part has four items.
First, the transformation of the acceptance of the meal is as stated in the text.
At that time, those nine million bodhisattvas all raised their voices and said:
I wish to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and also to see the assembly of bodhisattvas such as Vimalakīrti.

Although those members of the assembly have received the transformation of the Land of Fragrance, they also have a karmic affinity with the teachings for śrāvakas; therefore, I wish for them to go together with me.
The Buddha said, "You may go.
Restrain the fragrance of your body so that those sentient beings do not give rise to thoughts of delusion or attachment. This section on the instruction for permission to go consists of three parts.
"This was the first instance of restraining his bodily fragrance.
Kumārajīva said,
"If one is greatly enraged, one becomes insane."
Great joy is also delusive;
you should restrain your fragrance to prevent it from becoming a cause for confusion.
Furthermore, you must abandon your original form.
"Do not cause those in that country who seek the bodhisattva path to feel self-contempt or shame. This is the second [point], regarding the regulation of one's physical appearance.
Kumārajīva said:
"If shame is deep, it leads to death; if shame is shallow, it still causes distress."
When these two afflictions converge, one’s departure from the Way becomes ever more remote.
The former statement concerns deluded attachment; the latter concerns base shame. These two aspects are mutually revealed according to their respective texts.
Furthermore, you must not harbor thoughts of contempt or disdain toward them, nor conceive of them as obstacles.
Why is this? Because the lands of the ten directions are all like empty space.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, desiring to transform those who delight in inferior teachings, [manifest these worlds].
It is not that its pure lands are not fully manifested; rather, there are three reasons why the text contains admonitions against disparagement, which are explained as follows:
sentient beings in this Sahā world tend to treat those who are inferior with contempt, yet feel ashamed when they encounter those who are superior.
If one encounters a favorable opportunity, one should wear it; thus, by means of that [example], this is admonished.
When the manifested Bodhisattva had accepted the alms-bowl and the food,
Together with those nine million bodhisattvas,
they suddenly vanished from that world, sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the strength of Vimalakīrti.
In a brief moment, they arrived at the house of Vimalakīrti; the four classes of transformed beings came together as well.
Vimalakīrti then manifested nine million lion thrones, magnificent and beautiful just as before.
All the bodhisattvas sat upon them; this refers to the previous description of Vimalakīrti’s miraculous manifestation in the "Inconceivable" chapter.
Then, the manifested bodhisattva presented a bowl filled with fragrant food to Vimalakīrti.
The fragrance of the rice permeated the city of Vaiśālī as well as the trichiliocosm; these three aspects of the rice performed the work of a Buddha in two ways:
first, its fragrance, and later, its flavor.
Within the former [section], there are again three parts.
This fragrance pervasively perfumes;
it permeates the ten directions.
This is merely because the conditions of the three thousandfold world system should be thus.

At that time, the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, having smelled this fragrance, felt joy in both body and mind and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. This is the second instance of gaining benefit through smelling the fragrance.
Zhaò said:
"A rare fragrance entered his body, and his mind and person were filled with joy.
Thereupon, the elder Moon Canopy (Candraprabha)..."
Eighty-four thousand people came to enter the house of Vimalakīrti.
Upon entering, they saw that his chamber was filled with a great multitude of bodhisattvas and many lion thrones, all lofty, vast, and magnificently adorned.
All were filled with great joy; they paid homage to the assembly of bodhisattvas and the great disciples, then withdrew to stand to one side.
The earth spirits, the spirits of space, and the various devas of the desire and form realms did likewise.
Upon smelling this fragrance, they all came into Vimalakīrti’s house; those with karmic affinity for the three realms of existence gathered there.
Zao said:
"The kingdom of Vaiśālī had no sovereign ruler."
Only five hundred elders governed the affairs of state together;
because Candracchattra was esteemed by all, he was called the Lord.
All the earth deities below gathered only after they had smelled his fragrance.
Then Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas,
"Venerable sirs, you may eat this meal of the Tathāgata’s ambrosial flavor,
which has been permeated by great compassion."
Do not limit your intention, for that which is not digested by food [will cause harm]. This section below, consisting of four parts, concerns the ritual of eating as a Buddha-activity;
this first part is an exhortation to eat. Worldly food relies upon poisonous fangs.
"This rice has become nectar.
Śāṇakavāsin said, "Nirvāṇa is the Dharma of nectar; it is this that is eaten."
Because this food was obtained through such effort, there is the flavor of ambrosia within the rice.
As for that which is permeated by great compassion,
my heart’s response to it is such that the beings I may save have a limit.
Through the cultivation of great compassion, one's merit and wisdom become inexhaustible.
Those who eat should seek the fruit of Buddhahood to universally benefit all sentient beings.
If one restricts this to one's own person—seeking only self-regulation and self-deliverance—one turns one's back on the spirit of giving, and thus the food will not be digested.
There was another śrāvaka who thought:
"This food is meager, yet this great assembly must each eat it. This was the second [thought].
Zhaò said:
Because this inconceivable food is beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles, they gave rise to this thought.
The manifested bodhisattva said:
"Do not attempt to measure the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit and wisdom with the meager virtue and limited knowledge of a śrāvaka."
The four seas may run dry,
but this food is inexhaustible;
were all people to eat morsels from it, it would never be depleted.
Even if one were to spend an entire kalpa, from the time of Mount Sumeru until now, one could not exhaust [the faults].
The third section is the rebuke by the Bodhisattva of the Three Transformations.
This section has three parts.
This is the first censure.
The fruit of the śrāvakas' self-discipline is called "lesser virtue," whereas that of the Buddhas is the merit-retribution of great compassion.
The retributions for the fish and dragons of the four immeasurable oceans may be exhausted,
but the merit of this meal offered to the Buddhas is inexhaustible; therefore,
even if many people were to eat it for long kalpas, it would never be depleted.
It would never come to an end, just as Mount Sumeru never perishes. Why is this?
Because it is fully endowed with the merits of inexhaustible precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
That which remains after being eaten can never be exhausted. This second point explains the cause.
Zhaò says:
The retribution for the inexhaustible merit of the Tathāgata’s fivefold Dharma-body—how could such alms-food ever be exhausted?

Thereupon, the food in the bowl completely satisfied the entire assembly, yet it was not depleted. Even after three meals, it was not depleted. All those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans who ate this food [were likewise satisfied].
Their bodies are at ease and happy, like those bodhisattvas in the land of Sarva-sukha-vyūha (All Adornments of Happiness).

Furthermore, a wondrous fragrance issues from all their pores, just like the fragrance of the trees in the land of Gandhavatī (Possessing Fragrance). These four kinds of food thus benefit beings, enabling them to attain happiness and emit fragrances as described in the text.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas from the Fragrant Accumulation [Buddha-field]:

"In what manner does the Tathāgata Fragrant Accumulation teach the Dharma? This second section clarifies that the two lands—the pure and the defiled—differ in their Buddha-activities performed according to the conditions of those to be converted.
This was the first question concerning the Pure Land.
That bodhisattva said:
"In my land, the Tathāgata does not employ verbal discourse."
"By means of various fragrances, they cause all devas and humans to enter into the practice of the precepts (*vinaya*). These two answers concern the transformation of conditions:
those of shallow capacity enter into the practice of the precepts, while those of deep capacity become fully endowed with samādhi."
Zhaò said:
"That land is not entirely without speech;
it simply takes fragrance as the basis for the path of communication."

In this way, while some countries attain enlightenment through the path of verbal teaching, there are also those who attain it through the miraculous transformations of the country deities or other such matters.
Each of the Bodhisattvas sat beneath a fragrant tree and smelled this wondrous fragrance.
One immediately attains the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
For one who has attained this samādhi, all the merits possessed by a bodhisattva are fully perfected; it is equal to all samādhis.
Sengzhao said:
"The power of this samādhi is able to give rise to all meritorious virtues. That bodhisattva asked Vimalakīrti:
"Now, by what means does the World-Honored One Śākyamuni preach the Dharma? These two passages clarify the defiled land.
The text has four parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
Third is the praise;
fourth is the exposition.
This is the first [of the latter].
Vimalakīrti said:
"Because the sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform, the Buddha speaks words of sternness to subdue them. These are the two answers.
The text has three parts.
Within the first part, which consists of the Dharma, there are again three sections;
this is the initial heading.
Sengzhao said:
"How could the transformation of the Sage be fixed? It merely responds according to the nature of things.
Since the people of this land are stubborn and fierce, he responds to them with teachings that are likewise firm and fierce."
They say: "This is hell; this is the realm of animals; this is the realm of hungry ghosts;
these are the places of hardship;
these are the birthplaces of fools."
"This is bodily misconduct and this is the retribution for bodily misconduct;
this is verbal misconduct and this is the retribution for verbal misconduct;
this is mental misconduct and this is the retribution for mental misconduct. These two [sections] enumerate harsh speech.
The Lotus Sūtra uses words to penetrate the true reality (bhūtatathatā) and is therefore called the "Gentle Voice.

In contrast, everything from the beginning in the hells up to the distinctions between the mundane world and nirvāṇa is not speech that exhausts the principle of non-duality; thus, it is all termed "Harsh Speech."
The text briefly elucidates this through the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*).
Here, one who has attained the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), being free from the causes of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*) and free from rebirth in the three evil states,
encounters the Buddha-dharma, possesses correct faith, and practices— such a person is called a human vehicle (*manuṣyayāna*).
This is killing and this is the retribution for killing;
this is taking what is not given and this is the retribution for taking what is not given;
this is sexual misconduct and this is the retribution for sexual misconduct.
This is false speech and this is the retribution for false speech.
This is divisive speech and this is the retribution for divisive speech.
This is harsh speech and this is the retribution for harsh speech.
This is idle speech and this is the retribution for idle speech;
this is covetousness and envy and this is the retribution for covetousness and envy;
this is anger and malice and this is the retribution for anger and malice.

This is wrong view and this is the retribution for wrong view. If one does not commit these two along with the ten unwholesome deeds, then through the retribution of the ten wholesome karmas, one is born in the desire heavens; this is called the "vehicle of the gods" (*devayāna*).

If one further cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is born in the form realm heavens. As for double-tongued speech, it is speech that causes division; as for meaningless speech, it is speech that lacks purpose.
Kumārajīva said:
"The Hu (Sanskrit) original says:
'A miscellaneous discourse.'"
Furthermore, to engage in verbal karma that neither performs good deeds nor leads toward nirvana is entirely termed "mixed speech.
This is stinginess and cowardice; this is the retribution for stinginess and cowardice.
This is the violation of precepts; this is the retribution for violating precepts.
This is anger; this is the retribution for anger.
This is laziness; this is the retribution for laziness.
"This is a distracted mind; this is the retribution for a distracted mind.
This is delusion; this is the retribution for delusion. These three, when the six corruptions are eliminated and the six perfections are cultivated, constitute the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
This is the formulation of the precepts; this is the observance of the precepts; this is the violation of the precepts. This is what should be done; this is what should not be done.
This is an obstruction; this is not an obstruction.
"This is the incurrence of offense; this is the departure from offense. Below this, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are explained together.
The text is divided into three parts.
This first section concerns the training in the precepts.
Regarding "the formulation of precepts" (jie jie):
Zao says that according to the meaning of the Vinaya, this refers to the establishment of precepts based on specific events.
To comply with the instructions is called "upholding";
to oppose them is called "offending.
Because it is permitted, one should perform [the action].
Because it is a prescribed prohibition (*prajñapti-śīla*), one should not commit it;
yet, as a nature-precept (*prakṛti-śīla*), it does not obstruct the Path. Because it is a prohibited prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), it does not obstruct the precepts.
A transgression committed with a heavy mind constitutes a grave obstruction;
one committed with a light mind does not.
Because it is not confessed, one incurs guilt.
Through repentance, one is freed from transgressions.
Whether this be purity or defilement—these two belong to the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
Ordinary persons cultivate meditative concentration with a mind of attachment; for them, it constitutes defilement.
The noble ones cultivate the untainted mind for the sake of purity.
This [mind] is tainted; this is untainted.
This is the false path; this is the true path.
"This is conditioned; this is unconditioned.
This is the world; this is nirvana. The following clarifies the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
The seven types of noble persons (*saptāryapudgala*) possess outflows (*sāsrava*).
The eight noble, untainted [paths] constitute the eightfold right path;
to turn away from these is called the wrong path.
The three truths are conditioned;
the truth of cessation is unconditioned.
They comprise the three worlds and transcendence from the three worlds, which is nirvana.

Because the minds of those whose hearts are difficult to transform are like monkeys, one must govern their minds through various kinds of skillful means before they can be tamed. The concluding text below makes this clear.
For example, just as an elephant or horse that is unruly and untamed must be subjected to various forms of pain and suffering—even to the point of piercing the bone—before it is finally tamed;
so too, because sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform.
One may enter the discipline only through words that are entirely harsh and cutting; these are the two metaphors.
There are four ways to train a horse.
When a bodhisattva sees the whip, [he applies himself].
Those of the Two Vehicles touch the skin;
humans and devas touch the flesh;
it is said that the taming of the three evil realms reaches even to the bone.
The combined text makes this clear.
Zhaor said:
"Without the hook and the goad, there is no way to train elephants and horses."
"Without harsh words, there is no way to subdue those who are difficult to transform.
When those bodhisattvas heard this teaching,
they all exclaimed, "This is truly unprecedented!"
Just as the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha,
conceals his immeasurable power of mastery and instead delivers sentient beings by means of the dharmas they delight in through craving— this is the third praise.
The text has two parts;
this first section praises the Buddha.
Zhaò says:
The tracks of all Buddhas are equal, yet there appear to be disparities;
these disparities arise because sentient beings are inferior and their aspirations are narrow and small,
whereby the Buddha conceals his sovereign power to accord with their poverty and meanness.
He accords with what they delight in to bring them salvation;
his responsive manifestations are without fixed direction,
and he makes no distinction between the pure and the defiled.
This is truly unprecedented!
These bodhisattvas are also capable of such diligent humility;
they have come to this buddha-field out of immeasurable great compassion. This concludes the praise of the bodhisattvas who are visible.
Vimalakīrti said,
"The great compassion of the bodhisattvas in this land toward all sentient beings is indeed firm and steadfast,
just as you have said."

Nevertheless, the benefit to sentient beings achieved by this [practice] in a single lifetime exceeds that of practicing those [other methods] in that land for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. These four accounts are sincere;
they do not mention the Buddha because his power of the Way is already perfected.
The text has two parts.
This first section describes the benefits:
by deepening one's cultivation of the wholesome, the effort required becomes minimal.
"To transform the wicked, the merit is profound.
Ruyi said, "If one practices for a long time without achieving merit, is it not so?"
If it is near and beneficial, why is that?
Because in this Sahā world there are ten wholesome dharmas.
These are not found in any other pure lands.
What are the ten? First, one gathers in the poor through the practice of giving.
One gathers those who violate the precepts through pure ethical discipline; one gathers those who harbor ill will through patience;
one gathers those who are indolent through diligence;
and one gathers those with distracted minds through meditative concentration.
He gathers the ignorant through wisdom;
he teaches the Dharma for removing hardships to deliver those in the eight difficult conditions;
and he delivers those who delight in the Hīnayāna by means of the Mahāyāna.
He rescues those who have not attained [liberation] by means of all roots of goodness.
He constantly brings sentient beings to fulfillment through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
These are the twelve explanations of the reasons why.
The enumeration and explanation of the headings can be seen [in the text].
Zhaò said:
"Indeed, good arises from evil."
Purity increases when impurity is present;
because this land possesses the ten unwholesome dharmas, the ten virtues flourish there.
Because that land is purely wholesome, there is no ground for the virtue of giving to arise.
"Therefore, practicing for hundreds of thousands of kalpas is not equal to [practicing] for a single lifetime.
That bodhisattva asked:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva [attain this]?"
To practice the five sores within this world while being born in a pure land—this is the third [section] clarifying the conduct for the pure land.
The text has two parts;
this is the first, the question.
Zhaò said:
"He posed this question in order to encourage the novice bodhisattvas of this land to be reborn in a pure land.
Vimalakīrti then spoke:
If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they will act without blemish in this world and be born in a pure land. This second answer consists of four parts:
the heading, the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion.
This is the first heading.
What are the eight? This second inquiry is evident.
To benefit sentient beings without expecting a reward.
He undergoes all manner of suffering and afflictions on behalf of all sentient beings, dedicating all his merit entirely to them. Zhaò says:
"The Bodhisattva undergoes suffering on their behalf without regard for his own person."
All merits are bestowed entirely upon sentient beings;
how could one harbor thoughts of reward because they have been benefited?
If it were not for sentient beings, one would have long since entered nirvana.
To undergo suffering on their behalf so that they may be delivered first—
while they depart and I remain— is not a substitution;
what, then, is called the ultimate benefit?
This is the first dharma:
to regard all sentient beings with an impartial mind, being humble and without obstruction. Zhaò says:
"To make no distinction between enemies and kin."
To humble oneself and place others before one,
treating them with equal respect and without partiality—
these are the two dharmas.
Regarding all bodhisattvas as one regards a Buddha. Zhaò says:
"Bodhisattvas are the bridge for sentient beings and the link to the Triple Gem;
regarding them as Buddhas increases one's own merit."
The third dharma: to hear a sūtra not previously heard without harboring doubt. Zhaò says:
Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, one hears them and accepts them with faith;
one does not give rise to suspicion or confusion because they were not heard before.
These are the four dharmas.
They do not contradict the stage of the śrāvaka. ZHAO says:
Although the three vehicles differ, their ultimate destination is not distinct.
Not to oppose others on account of their status, whether high or low—
this is the fifth dharma.
Not to envy the offerings received by others nor to exalt one's own gains.
And therein one should discipline the mind. Zhaò says:
"If another plants and another reaps, why be envious?
If one plants and one reaps, why be arrogant?"
Thus, to skillfully discipline oneself within these two [aspects] is the sixth method.
Constantly examining one’s own faults and not disputing the shortcomings of others. Zhaò says:
To examine one's own faults, and the faults will naturally vanish;

the Buddha rejoices in your words. These two lines of praise by the Buddhas are to be understood according to the text.
Then all these bodhisattvas joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
shall widely proclaim and disseminate the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi throughout the lands of the ten directions."

Furthermore, one should guide and instruct all those who preach the Dharma so that they may obtain this sutra. Second, because the Bodhisattvas receive the lamp of the Dharma and illuminate everywhere, they vow to proclaim it throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
wherever there may be cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, or wildernesses,
and wherever there are those who read, recite, explain, and expound this sutra scroll—
"I shall lead my officials and subordinates to visit his location for the sake of hearing the Dharma and provisionally protect that person;

for a hundred yojanas around, I will ensure that no one seeks to find an opportunity to harm him. Below this, in the third and fourth volumes of the *Sūtra on the Four Heavenly Kings Receiving the Imperial Decree*, it is stated that the calamities of their dwelling places are naturally purified.
Moreover, as the divine powers provide protection and sustenance, the propagation of the Dharma will increase even further.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive and uphold this sutra, and widely proclaim and disseminate it."
Ānanda said, "Yes,
World-Honored One; I have already received and upheld the essentials."
"What should this sutra be named?
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda,"
This sutra is titled "The Teaching of Vimalakīrti," and it is also titled "The Dharma-Gate of the Inconceivable Liberation.
Thus should it be upheld. [The following two sections concern the entrustment to Ānanda, the transmission, and the questions and answers.]
If one were to ensure that nothing was omitted at the time of the compilation,
[it would be as follows]: after the Buddha had spoken this sutra,
the elder Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others...
The entire great assembly, including the devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
Below this, it is stated that the entrustment was completed, and they celebrated hearing [the teaching] and vowed to practice and uphold it.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Lower, Compiled in Guanzhong.
